It's over-18s only and lasts about two and a half hours, rain or shine.
cosaSiFa: Meet in front of Toledo metro station, on Via Toledo. From there you walk towards the old town. The group stops at three or four bars chosen because Neapolitans actually drink there and prices are local; the guide points out the best deals and tells you where it's worth paying cash.

Between bars you cross the squares where street musicians play in the evening, and the guide gets everyone playing group games, some of them fairly odd, to get strangers talking. The route goes as far as the Quartieri Spagnoli. If you're hungry, grab a pizza a portafoglio (a pizza folded in four) on the street.

If you want a late one, at the end of the crawl you can be taken to a nightclub, with a separate entry fee paid on the door that includes a cocktail. Drinks along the way are paid for at the bar. About 150 minutes in all.
486452.perChi: For solo travellers or couples who want to meet people, and for groups of friends who don't know where to go on their first night. Over-18s only. Not for anyone after a quiet evening or wanting to learn the history of the lanes: here you drink, play games and walk. Sandals and flip-flops aren't allowed.
486452.consiglio: Have dinner first, or factor in a pizza a portafoglio: it's a boozy outing. Carry cash for the best deals. Toledo metro is easy to reach and, before you start, the station itself and Via Toledo are worth a look. Book ahead at weekends, it fills up.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long does it last?
faq.a: The meeting point is Toledo metro station, in central Naples. The crawl lasts about 150 minutes, is done on foot and goes ahead in any weather, rain included.

faq.q: Are drinks included?
faq.a: The booking platform lists the guide and drinks as included, but the tour description makes clear that drinks and shots are paid for at the bars, where you'll find deals at local prices. Entry to the optional nightclub at the end is extra. Check what's included when you book.

faq.q: Minimum age, languages and cancellation?
faq.a: Over-18s only: under-18s can't take part. The guide speaks English and Italian. Cancel for free up to 24 hours before with a full refund. No sandals or flip-flops.

489189.intro: An afternoon at a dairy that has been making mozzarella and cheeses for more than fifty years, a few minutes from the centre of Naples. You follow every stage of the process, from heating the curd to stretching it, and try pulling the mozzarella apart with your own hands. Then you move out to a garden of lemon trees and roses to cook a southern Italian dish together and taste the house cheeses, a ricotta and lemon tiramisù and homemade limoncello.
cosaSiFa: You meet at Rione Alto metro station, easy to reach from the centre. From there it’s a five-minute drive to the dairy, which has been making mozzarella and traditional cheeses for over fifty years. The first part happens in the workshop: you watch how mozzarella is born, step by step, from heating to stretching, and everyone gets to pull it apart themselves.

Then you move into the garden, among lemon trees and roses. Together you prepare a typical southern Italian dish, taste the freshly made cheeses and finish with the house tiramisù, made with ricotta and fresh lemons, and a small glass of limoncello. Two and a half hours in all, with food and drinks included. You’re brought back to Rione Alto at the end.
489189.perChi: For anyone who wants to see how mozzarella is really made and sit down to eat with the people who make it, well away from the tourist circuit. The venue is wheelchair accessible and there’s a small-group or private option. Less suited to anyone after a quick activity in the centre: you do have to get yourself to Rione Alto.
489189.consiglio: Come hungry, because the meal is generous. The metro is the easiest way to reach the meeting point; a taxi back to your hotel isn’t included. Dates go quickly, so book a few days ahead.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long does it last?
faq.a: You meet at Rione Alto metro station, and the dairy is a five-minute drive from there. The activity lasts about two and a half hours between workshop, garden and tasting, and you’re brought back to the same spot.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The mozzarella class, cooking the dish in the garden and the whole tasting: cheeses, tiramisù and limoncello, with food and drinks included. A taxi or private transfer from your hotel isn’t included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The activity runs in Italian or English, depending on the date you choose. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later.

561524.intro: Two hours in the Capodimonte Museum with an art historian and a small group, ticket included. The museum holds Caravaggio, Raphael, Titian and room after room of other masterpieces: on your own it’s easy to walk past the right paintings without noticing. With someone who knows them, in two hours you go straight to the key works and understand the context and story of each one. The tour is in Italian and you meet at the Porta Grande of the park.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the Porta Grande of the Bosco di Capodimonte, the main gate of the park, and walk from there to the museum. Tickets have already been arranged by the organisers, so you go straight in.

Inside, the art historian takes the group to the main works: the Caravaggios, the Raphaels, the Titians and the other highlights of the collection, pointing out the details to look for, the historical context and the stories behind the paintings. It isn’t a rush through the rooms: the stops are chosen, and you stay in front of each work as long as it needs. The group is small, so you can ask questions and pause where you’re interested.
The visit lasts two hours and ends back at the Porta Grande. The guide speaks Italian. The route isn’t suitable for anyone with limited mobility or using a wheelchair.
561524.perChi: For painting lovers who want a serious guided visit in Italian, without the noise of big groups. Good for couples and for anyone back in Naples who has already seen the centre. Less suited to anyone after a quick stroll or travelling with small children. The route isn’t wheelchair accessible.
561524.consiglio: Capodimonte is outside the centre: allow time to get there by bus or taxi and don’t arrive in a rush. After the museum, the park is the place to sit on the grass, and the neighbourhood below, the Sanità, is worth the rest of the day. Book in time, the tour often sells out.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long does it last?
faq.a: The meeting point is the Porta Grande of the Bosco e Museo di Capodimonte. The visit lasts 2 hours and ends back at the same spot. The group is small, so you can talk to the guide and linger in front of the paintings.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The museum entry ticket and two hours with an art historian as your guide. Tickets are arranged in advance by the organisers. Transport to Capodimonte, food and drinks aren’t included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The visit is in Italian. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. After that, the ticket isn’t refunded.

590725.intro: Two and a half hours on foot through monumental Naples, in a small group, with an hour inside the Palazzo Reale, the Royal Palace. You start at the Fountain of Neptune in Piazza Municipio, pass the Maschio Angioino, walk through the Galleria Umberto, stop outside the San Carlo opera house and reach Piazza del Plebiscito; then the royal apartments. You finish with a stroll through the old Santa Lucia quarter and along the seafront to Castel dell’Ovo. Guide in Italian, English or French, palace ticket included.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Municipio, at the Fountain of Neptune. First stop is Castel Nuovo, the Maschio Angioino, seen from outside with ten minutes of explanation. You cross the Galleria Umberto I and arrive in front of the Teatro di San Carlo, then Piazza del Plebiscito. Each stop lasts about ten minutes, just enough to understand what you’re looking at.

The heart of the tour is the Palazzo Reale: you go in with the ticket included and spend about an hour inside, through the richly decorated rooms of the royal apartments and the historic collections, while the guide tells you who lived there and how.

Out of the palace you walk down Via Santa Lucia, with a quarter of an hour on the story of the old neighbourhood, to the seafront. The last ten minutes are a stroll with Vesuvius ahead of you to Castel dell’Ovo, where the tour ends.
590725.perChi: Good for first-timers in Naples who want to see the landmark sights with someone explaining them, without rushing. The group is small and the pace relaxed. You’re walking the whole time, so it isn’t suitable for anyone with limited mobility or using a wheelchair; no suitcases or large bags.
590725.consiglio: The tour ends below Castel dell’Ovo: from there the pedestrian seafront along Via Caracciolo is the natural next step, all the way to Mergellina. Comfortable shoes and, in summer, the morning slot: Piazza del Plebiscito at midday has no shade. Choose your language when you book, because the tours are separate and often sell out.

faq.q: Where does it start and finish?
faq.a: It starts at the Fountain of Neptune in Piazza Municipio and ends near Castel dell’Ovo, on the seafront. The whole route is on foot and lasts about two and a half hours, one hour of it inside the Palazzo Reale.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The local guide and the entry ticket to the Palazzo Reale. The other landmarks, the Maschio Angioino, Galleria Umberto, San Carlo and Piazza del Plebiscito, are seen from outside. Transport, food and drinks aren’t included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: There are separate tours in Italian, English and French: you choose the language when you book. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. The tour often sells out, so it’s best to book early.

623340.intro: The simplest way to see Positano and Amalfi in a day: an air-conditioned coach from Naples with an assistant on board, an audio guide in five languages, three free hours in Positano and two in Amalfi. From April to October you travel between the two towns by ferry, half an hour of coastline seen from the water; in winter you go by coach. Pick-up is from stops in central Naples, including Molo Beverello, Via Toledo and Piazza Bovio.
cosaSiFa: You board the coach at one of the stops in the centre, the first at Molo Beverello, early in the morning. An hour and a half on the road and you’re in Positano. Here you have three hours to yourself: down to the beaches, the vertical lanes, the church of Santa Maria Assunta with its majolica-tiled dome, a coffee by the sea. The audio guide tells you what you’re looking at.

In the afternoon you move on to Amalfi. In summer the trip is by ferry, about thirty minutes with the Amalfi Coast sliding past; from November to March the coach takes you. In Amalfi you have two free hours for the cathedral of Sant’Andrea, the square and the shops full of lemons and limoncello. Then an hour and a half by coach and you’re back in Naples, at the same stops.
623340.perChi: For anyone who wants to spend sensibly and have plenty of free time: there’s no guided walking tour here, just an assistant on the coach and an audio guide, and then you’re on your own. Good for families and for people who like exploring by themselves. If you want a guide explaining every corner, or a small group, look elsewhere.
623340.consiglio: The stops have fixed times and the coach doesn’t wait: be there five or ten minutes early. If you get seasick, bear in mind that the summer ferry depends on sea conditions and can be cancelled. Three hours in Positano is enough for a swim: bring your swimsuit. Lunch in Amalfi or Positano, your choice.

faq.q: Where does it leave from and at what time?
faq.a: The stops are in central Naples: Molo Beverello, Via Monteoliveto, Via Toledo, Via Medina, Via San Carlo, Piazza Bovio, Corso Lucci and Via Ferraris. You leave early in the morning and get back in the late afternoon, with times that can shift because of traffic or weather.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The assistant on board speaks English and Italian. The audio guide is included and comes in English, French, German, Spanish and Italian. There’s no guided walking tour in the towns: at each stop you’re free to wander as you like and manage your own time.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Return air-conditioned coach, the ferry from Positano to Amalfi in the summer season, the assistant on board and free time in both towns. Hotel pick-up, entry tickets and personal expenses aren’t included. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

644605.intro: Sant’Aspreno ai Crociferi is a 17th-century church, rebuilt in the 18th, at the start of the Borgo dei Vergini in the Rione Sanità. Closed for forty years, in 2021 it became the studio of the sculptor Jago, and since 2023 it has been a museum of his work, above all his Pietà. The guided visit lasts 25 minutes, is wheelchair accessible and is run by young people from the neighbourhood. Rated 4.9 on nearly three hundred reviews.
cosaSiFa: You check in at the ticket desk fifteen minutes before your time slot. You’ll recognise the church by its stucco façade and its lava-stone staircase, raised on purpose to protect it from the «lava dei Vergini», the torrent of rainwater and mud that used to pour down through the Sanità. It was built in 1633, dedicated to the first bishop of Naples, and rebuilt in 1760 by two of Vanvitelli’s collaborators.

Inside, the Latin-cross plan, with a single nave and two chapels on each side, holds Jago’s sculptures. The life-size Pietà was made right here, when the church was his studio; next to it stands Aiace e Cassandra (Ajax and Cassandra). The guide talks you through the works and the idea behind the reopening: reviving the neighbourhood through art.

After 25 minutes you’re out. But the ticket gets you two more things: free entry, by reservation, to Jago’s Gesù Bambino Velato (the Veiled Christ Child) in the Chapel of the Arciconfraternita dei Bianchi, and a reduced rate for the Catacombs of San Gennaro and San Gaudioso, which are in the same neighbourhood and round off the day.
644605.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants a reason to step into the Sanità: in half an hour you see something that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Good for families with older kids, who come across as engaged in the reviews, and for wheelchair users, since the visit is listed as accessible. If you want a long, detailed visit on every work, you’ll leave with a few questions.
644605.consiglio: Go in the morning and use it to open a day in the Sanità: afterwards, with the ticket discount, the Catacombs of San Gennaro or San Gaudioso, and a stop in the Borgo dei Vergini. Book the Gesù Bambino Velato at the Bianchi too: it’s included but has to be requested. Be on time: latecomers aren’t let in and aren’t refunded.

faq.q: How long does it last and in what language?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts 25 minutes and is available in Italian or English, chosen when you book. You need to be at the ticket desk fifteen minutes before your time slot; the ticket is valid only for that day and time, and latecomers can’t join later slots.

faq.q: Is it wheelchair accessible?
faq.a: Yes, the operator lists the visit as wheelchair accessible. The route is short: Jago’s sculptures are in the nave and in the church’s two side chapels on each side, and the guided visit lasts 25 minutes in all.

faq.q: What does the ticket include?
faq.a: Entry and the guided visit of the church and museum. On top of that, after the visit you can book free entry to Jago’s Gesù Bambino Velato in the Chapel of the Arciconfraternita dei Bianchi, and you get a reduced rate for the Catacombs of San Gennaro and San Gaudioso. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

702971.intro: A boat just for your group, with a skipper, leaving from Borgo Marinari and following the Posillipo coast to the Gaiola. You pass below Castel dell’Ovo and in front of Mergellina, then along the caves and clifftop villas of Posillipo to the fishing village of Marechiaro and the little island of the Gaiola. On the way you stop for a swim, with masks to look underwater. You choose the length when you book, from half an hour to three hours. Nine people maximum.
cosaSiFa: You board at the little harbour of Borgo Marinari, at the foot of Castel dell’Ovo, or at the second departure point used by some options. The skipper doubles as your guide: as you leave the harbour he talks about the castle and the city seen from the water, then points the bow towards Mergellina and the hill of Posillipo.

Along Posillipo you go slowly, close to the shore, to see the caves and the historic villas facing the sea, including Villa Lauro and Villa Volpicelli. You reach Marechiaro, the fishing village, and then the Gaiola islet. Here, weather permitting, you stop to swim and snorkel with the masks provided on board.

Drinking water is on board. Options range from half an hour to three hours; if the swim matters to you, choose carefully, because several guests would have liked more time in the water. You return to the same point you left from, with the skipper still telling myths and stories of the coast.
702971.perChi: For anyone who wants the sea without the crowd: the boat is private, nine people at most, so it works for couples, families and groups of friends. You need to be comfortable on a small boat. The operator doesn’t allow children under three, pregnant women, anyone over seventy, anyone weighing over 140 kg or with breathing problems.
702971.consiglio: Swimsuit on underneath, towel and sun cream: the swim stop comes with no changing room. Late afternoon, with the low light on Posillipo, is the best time for photos. Before or after, take a walk around Borgo Marinari and along the seafront, which are right there.

faq.q: How long is the boat trip?
faq.a: It depends on the option: from half an hour up to three hours. The longer options leave more time for the swim stop at the Gaiola. You leave from and return to the same point, usually Borgo Marinari, below Castel dell’Ovo.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: A skipper who also acts as guide, snorkel masks, bottled water and fuel. The boat is reserved for your group, up to nine people. The skipper speaks Italian and English. The meeting point can change depending on the option you choose.

faq.q: Are there age or health restrictions?
faq.a: Yes. It isn’t suitable for children under three, pregnant women, people over seventy, anyone weighing more than 140 kg, with breathing problems or who has had recent surgery. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

747476.intro: The easiest way to understand Posillipo: from the sea. You set off from the pier on Via Caracciolo and follow the hill where, since Roman times, anyone who could afford it built a villa to be left in peace. Along the way the boat stops for swimming and snorkelling in protected waters, with masks on board, music and soft drinks. There are 1.5-hour and 3-hour versions, shared or private. Rated 4.9.
cosaSiFa: You board at the pier on the Via Caracciolo seafront and head out towards Posillipo. Whoever is at the helm tells you about what you see on the coast: the villas, the ancient ruins, the myths tied to the name of the place, which in Greek means roughly «where pain ends».

The stops are the best part. You drop anchor in coves and stretches of protected sea, climb down for a swim and, if you like, use the snorkel masks kept on board. Between stops there’s water, soft drinks and beer; on the private versions there’s also prosecco for a toast.

The basic trip lasts an hour and a half; the three-hour one goes further along the coast. There are semi-private options, in a group, and private ones; there’s also a two-hour private sunset trip. You return to the same pier. The trip needs a minimum of six people to run: otherwise you’re offered an alternative or a refund.
747476.perChi: For anyone who wants a swim in Naples without hunting for a beach, and for those who have seen the centre and want a different afternoon. Good with friends and as a couple; works with kids who can swim. Not suitable for wheelchair users. Short on time, pick the hour-and-a-half version; if you can, go for the three hours.
747476.consiglio: Beach towels on board are rented for a fee, cash only: bring your own. Swimsuit already on, sun cream and a dry change of clothes for the way back. Pair the trip with a walk along the seafront or a coffee in Mergellina before boarding. In summer book a few days ahead: places are few and the minimum number is needed.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it leave from?
faq.a: You leave from the pier on Via Caracciolo, on the Naples seafront, and come back to the same spot. You choose between an hour and a half and three hours, shared or private, plus a two-hour private sunset option.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The trip along the coast, the stops for swimming and snorkelling, the masks, and drinks on board: water, soft drinks and beer. Prosecco is only on the private options. Tips and towel rental are extra.

faq.q: What language do they speak on board, and can I cancel?
faq.a: Commentary is in English, Italian or Spanish. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before. Note: a minimum of 6 participants is needed; if it isn’t reached, the organisers offer another date or a full refund.

765797.intro: A three-hour class to make a Neapolitan calzone, not the usual round pizza, and a tiramisù with decaf coffee. You work the dough by hand, no rolling pin, fill and close the calzone, bake it in the wood-fired oven and then sit down to eat the lot with a drink. Small group, a local chef, recipes and a diploma to take home.
cosaSiFa: You start with the tiramisù, so it can rest while you work on the rest: mascarpone cream, biscuits dipped in decaf coffee, layers and cocoa. The chef shows you how thick the cream should be and how to balance biscuits, cream and cocoa so the dessert holds its shape.

Then the dough: you knead, shape and stretch it all by hand, using the techniques of pizza makers. Instead of a disc, you make a calzone: you add the filling, fold it over and learn to seal the edges so nothing escapes while it bakes.

The calzone goes into the wood-fired oven and you watch it puff up and colour. Then to the table: the calzone fresh from the oven with a drink, alcoholic or not, water throughout and, to finish, the tiramisù, which has been resting in the meantime. You leave with the written recipes and a diploma.
765797.perChi: For anyone who has already done a pizza class and wants something different, or who doesn’t drink coffee: the tiramisù is decaf. Small group, time for questions. Under-18s only with a parent or guardian. Three hours standing at the counter, and no wheelchair access.
765797.consiglio: Do it at lunch or dinner time and arrive hungry: calzone and tiramisù are filling. Dress for the kitchen, not for a night out, flour sticks. The meeting point is on Via delle Zite, a fifteen-minute walk from the central station and the Duomo: afterwards, the old town is just round the corner.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The chef for the whole class, apron and utensils, the ingredients for calzone and tiramisù, baking in the wood-fired oven, the meal with your own calzone and dessert, one alcoholic or soft drink, water, the recipes and the diploma.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: English, Italian and French; you choose the language when booking. It lasts three hours.

faq.q: Can I cancel, and where do we meet?
faq.a: Free cancellation up to 24 hours before. Under-18s must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. The meeting point is on Via delle Zite.

833595.intro: Thirty-five minutes inside the Cappella Sansevero with a guide, ticket already included and guaranteed entry, with no queue at the ticket office. You meet at the obelisk in Piazza San Domenico Maggiore and two minutes later you’re inside. You see the Cristo Velato (the Veiled Christ), the chapel’s other statues such as Modesty and Disillusion, and the Anatomical Machines. It’s the right visit if you have half an hour and want to be sure of getting in.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is the obelisk in the middle of Piazza San Domenico Maggiore. From there the guide takes the group to the chapel, two minutes’ walk away, and you go in with the ticket already booked. If the group is larger than ten, headsets are handed out so you can hear the explanation even when it’s crowded.

Inside, the guide tells the story of Raimondo di Sangro and his chapel, then the Veiled Christ, with the details of the marble veil, and the other statues: Modesty and Disillusion. Finally you see the Anatomical Machines. Thirty-five minutes in all: it’s a focused visit, and anyone who wants to linger in front of the Christ will find it tight.
833595.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants guaranteed entry with commentary in Italian or Spanish. Fine for families, but everyone pays for a ticket, children included, and pushchairs aren’t allowed in. Not suitable for anyone with limited mobility or in a wheelchair. If you want to contemplate at leisure, choose a longer visit.
833595.consiglio: Don’t bring large backpacks or luggage: they’re not allowed, and neither is photography inside. Book ahead and check you’ve picked the right language. Afterwards the square is the perfect spot for a coffee and for carrying on along Spaccanapoli towards San Gregorio Armeno or Piazza del Gesù.

faq.q: Is the ticket included, and do I skip the queue?
faq.a: Yes, the entry ticket to the Cappella Sansevero is included and access is priority, without going through the ticket office. The guide is included too, as are headsets for groups of more than ten, so you can follow better.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts 35 minutes. The meeting point is the obelisk in Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, two minutes’ walk from the chapel. The tour ends at the chapel itself, in the heart of the old town.

faq.q: What isn’t allowed?
faq.a: Pets, large luggage, pushchairs and photography inside. All participants, of any age, must have a ticket. Languages available: Italian and Spanish. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

888244.intro: A tasting tour that leaves the tourist centre for the Sanità, the neighbourhood behind Porta San Gennaro where Neapolitans still do their shopping at the Vergini market. In two and a half hours, in English, you eat pizza margherita, mozzarella, taralli, sfogliatella and babà with wine, beer and limoncello, while looking at the murals and, from outside, the Palazzo dello Spagnuolo. You start and finish at Porta San Gennaro. It’s the right tour if you’ve already seen Spaccanapoli and want everyday Naples.
cosaSiFa: You meet at Porta San Gennaro, one of the old city gates, where the guide explains who San Gennaro is and why he matters so much here. The first stop is a tasting straight away, then you enter the Rione Sanità. You walk through the Vergini market, open in the mornings only, among stalls of vegetables and fish and the shouts of the vendors.

From the market you reach the Palazzo dello Spagnuolo, a 17th-century Baroque palace, seen from outside. Then stops in neighbourhood places alternate with stretches on foot among the Sanità’s murals: pizza margherita, fresh mozzarella, crunchy taralli, with local wine and beer. The guide talks about life in the neighbourhood and the people who live there.

You finish with something sweet, sfogliatella or babà, and limoncello. The route is a loop and you’re back at Porta San Gennaro after about two and a half hours. The exact stops aren’t announced in advance and may change, but the number of tastings stays the same. Children can only take part with an adult.
888244.perChi: For English speakers who aren’t on their first visit, or for anyone who wants to start with the less touristy side of Naples: couples, friends, families with accompanied kids. Fine for vegetarians too, if they say so when booking. Not suitable for coeliacs or anyone gluten intolerant, as there are no gluten-free alternatives.
888244.consiglio: Choose a morning slot if you want to catch the Vergini market in full swing, because it closes in the afternoon. Comfortable shoes and an empty stomach. You’re a few steps from the Catacombs of San Gennaro and from the Basilica della Sanità with the Catacombs of San Gaudioso: worth combining them to make a full half-day of the neighbourhood.

faq.q: What do we taste and what’s included?
faq.a: The guide, the walk and everything you eat and drink are included: pizza margherita, mozzarella, taralli, sfogliatella, babà, with wine, beer and limoncello. Anyone with allergies or intolerances must say so in advance. There are no gluten-free options.

faq.q: What language is the tour in and how long does it last?
faq.a: The tour is in English and lasts about two and a half hours. You start and finish at Porta San Gennaro, so there’s no need to arrange your way back from another part of the city. The stops are on foot, with short stretches between them.

faq.q: Can I bring children? Can I cancel?
faq.a: Children are welcome only if accompanied by an adult; unaccompanied minors aren’t. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later. The tour often sells out, so it’s best to move early.

919794.intro: Two hours on the Vomero hill, with a guide in Italian and entry tickets included, for the two monuments that stand side by side: the Certosa di San Martino and Castel Sant’Elmo. The Certosa, a former monastery, holds the nativity scene collection, the cloisters, the Bourbon carriages and boats and the Prior’s Quarters with the model of the Cristo Velato; at the castle, the largest fortress in the city, you climb up to the terraces where you can see everything: the bay, Vesuvius, Posillipo.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is Largo San Martino, the viewpoint in front of the Certosa. The visit to the monastery lasts about fifty minutes: you go through the nativity scene section, the cloister, the rooms with the Bourbon carriages and ships and the Prior’s Quarters, where the model of the Veiled Christ is kept. You finish on the terrace overlooking the bay.

Five minutes on foot and you’re at Castel Sant’Elmo. Here the guide spends an hour on the history of the fortress, you pass through the contemporary art installations and climb to the top, where you stop for photos: the old town below, Vesuvius, the Posillipo coast. The tour ends at the castle.
919794.perChi: Good for anyone who wants the view with some history too, and for those who have already seen the centre and want a different side of the city. Italian only. The walking is moderate, with stairs and slopes: not suitable for anyone with limited mobility or in a wheelchair. Holds up well with kids, between nativity scenes and a castle.
919794.consiglio: Bring ID, which you’ll be asked for, and water. Go up to the Vomero on the Funicolare Centrale from Via Toledo or on the Montesanto funicular, and walk back down the Pedamentina, the long stairway that leads to Corso Vittorio Emanuele. Late afternoon has the best light on the bay.

faq.q: Are entry tickets included?
faq.a: Yes, tickets for both the Certosa di San Martino and Castel Sant’Elmo are included, along with the guide. Transport, food and drinks and personal expenses aren’t included. Bring an ID document.

faq.q: How long does it last and how is the time split?
faq.a: Two hours in all: about fifty minutes in the Certosa and its cloisters, five minutes on foot, then an hour at Castel Sant’Elmo with a stop for photos over the bay. You start at Largo San Martino and finish at the castle.

faq.q: What language is it in and what should I bring?
faq.a: Italian only. You’ll need comfortable shoes, water and an ID document. Check the weather and, if needed, bring a raincoat. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

937692.intro: Half a day in Pompeii with nothing to worry about: an air-conditioned coach picks you up in Naples, your entry ticket is already sorted and inside the site you walk with an archaeologist as your guide. In three and a half hours you see the paved streets, the villas with their mosaics, the shops, the graffiti on the walls and the lupanar, the ancient brothel. The right amount of time if you don’t want to spend a whole day on the site but want to really understand it.
cosaSiFa: Pick-up is between thirty and fifty-five minutes before the activity starts, and there’s commentary on board on the way to Pompeii. Everyone gets a bottle of water. On arrival there’s no queue at the ticket office: tickets are included and the archaeologist guide meets the group at the entrance to the ruins.

Inside, the visit follows the cobbled streets past patrician houses and mosaics, shops and eateries of the time, with the writing on the walls and the lupanar as windows onto daily life up to AD 79. The guide explains in Italian or English, depending on the date. After the visit, the coach takes everyone back to Naples.
937692.perChi: For anyone who wants Pompeii with a proper explanation, without sorting out trains and tickets, and for those short on time: three and a half hours is a morning or an afternoon. Good if you’re staying in Naples, as pick-up is included. If you want to spend a whole day there exploring on your own, a simple ticket will suit you better.
937692.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and water: there’s little shade in Pompeii and the streets are stone. Keep your phone on in the morning: pick-up can come almost an hour before the start time. Tips for the guide aren’t included. If you want the afternoon free, round off the trip with a pizza near the station.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it leave from?
faq.a: Three and a half hours in all, pick-up included. The coach collects you in Naples between thirty and fifty-five minutes before the activity starts, and brings you back in the same vehicle after the visit.

faq.q: What language is the guide in?
faq.a: The archaeologist guide speaks Italian or English, depending on the date you choose when booking. There’s also commentary on the coach on the way to the ruins, so you arrive with some background already.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: An archaeologist guide at Pompeii, the entry ticket, a return air-conditioned coach, commentary on board and a bottle of water. Tips aren’t included. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with the option to book now and pay later.

947446.intro: Two hours in the old town to take home two Neapolitan crafts: first the pizza Margherita, from dough to baking in the traditional oven, then gelato, made with fresh seasonal ingredients. It’s the shortest of the workshops we list and the best one for children: you’re on your feet, you get your hands dirty and you eat what comes out. At the end you get a certificate and the recipes.
cosaSiFa: You arrive ten minutes early to register, put on an apron and hat and start with the dough: flour, water, yeast and salt worked into a ball. Meanwhile you make the sauce with San Marzano tomatoes. The pizzaiolo explains rising and proving, in other words why one Neapolitan pizza comes out soft and another doesn’t.

Then you stretch the base by hand, top it as a Margherita and bake it in the traditional Neapolitan oven. As soon as it comes out you eat it at the table, with a choice of red or white wine, beer or soft drinks. The second part is the gelato: you start from fresh ingredients and follow the process through to the end, with the techniques that set it apart from industrial ice cream.

You finish by tasting the freshly made gelato and receiving a pizzaiolo certificate with your name on it, along with the pizza and gelato recipes to try again at home. Two hours in all, the right length not to tire out little ones and to leave the rest of the day free.
947446.perChi: The right class for families with children: the operator lists it as suitable for them, it lasts two hours and gelato is a good incentive. Works for couples and groups of friends too. Under-18s must be with an adult. You work standing up the whole time and the room isn’t wheelchair accessible.
947446.consiglio: Comfortable clothes and closed shoes, because you’re on your feet and flour flies. The exact meeting point depends on the option you book and comes with your confirmation, but it’s always in the old town: at just two hours, it pairs well with a morning on Spaccanapoli or at the Archaeological Museum. It often sells out, book ahead.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children?
faq.a: Yes, the operator lists the class as suitable for families and children, and it lasts two hours. Under-18s must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. You work standing up the whole time, so wear comfortable clothes and shoes.

faq.q: What’s included and what language is it in?
faq.a: All the ingredients for pizza and gelato, the instructor, a disposable hat and apron, alcoholic and soft drinks, a personalised certificate and the recipes to take home. The pizzaiolo speaks English, French, Spanish and Italian; you choose the language when booking.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. Remember to arrive ten minutes before your booked time to register. Available times show up when you select a date while booking.

960715.intro: A three-hour class in the old town where everyone makes their own Neapolitan pizza from start to finish: dough, San Marzano tomato sauce, stretching by hand and baking in the traditional oven with the peel. Along the way you put together a tiramisù, which you then eat with a sip of limoncello. With more than sixteen hundred reviews and an average of 4.9, it’s the most-booked of the workshops we list. No cooking experience needed.
cosaSiFa: You start with an apron and hat, a Neapolitan starter to break the ice, and your hands in the dough: flour, water, salt and yeast worked into a ball. Then you prepare the San Marzano tomatoes for the sauce. Meanwhile the chef tells you where pizza and tiramisù come from, and corrects anyone kneading badly.

The most fun part is the stretching: widening the base with your fingers, getting it round, topping it and sliding it into the oven on the peel without dropping it. The crust puffs up in seconds before your eyes. In the meantime you layer up the tiramisù, with the final dusting of cocoa done your own way.

You sit down and eat your own pizza with a choice of soft drink, beer or a glass of wine, unlimited water, and the tiramisù with a taste of limoncello. At the end you leave with a certificate in your name, the recipes to make it all again at home and an instant photo with the chef.
960715.perChi: For anyone, from complete beginners to people who already make dough at home and want to understand the Neapolitan oven. Works for couples, groups of friends and families, with under-18s accompanied by an adult. Vegetarian options are available if you let them know in advance. Not wheelchair accessible, and you’re on your feet for much of the three hours.
960715.consiglio: Dress light: rooms with the oven going get hot, and several reviews mention it. Closed, comfortable shoes, nothing you care about wearing, flour gets everywhere. The exact meeting point depends on the option and comes with your confirmation, always in the old town: afterwards, Spaccanapoli and Via dei Tribunali are close by to walk it off.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: The chef instructor speaks Italian, French, Spanish and English; you choose the language when booking. The class lasts three hours and needs no previous experience: you learn the dough, the sauce, stretching, baking with the peel and the tiramisù.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: All ingredients and equipment, a disposable hat and apron, a typical Neapolitan starter, the pizza and tiramisù you make, a drink of your choice from soft drink, beer and wine, unlimited water, a taste of limoncello, the personalised certificate, the recipes and an instant photo.

faq.q: Is it good for children and families? Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes, under-18s can take part if accompanied by a parent or guardian. No pets allowed and no smoking inside. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later.

1032625.intro: A cooking class in a restaurant in the centre, a short walk from the port and the Teatro San Carlo, where you learn fresh pasta from scratch and tiramisù step by step. You start with a glass of prosecco and a Neapolitan starter, cook with the apron and tools provided, and at the end you eat what you’ve made, with a tasting of limoncello or coffee and amaro (a herbal liqueur). The group is small, and the class comes with a certificate and digital recipes. It runs every day except Sunday.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the restaurant. It starts with a welcome glass, prosecco or alcohol-free, and a Neapolitan starter, while the pastry chef who runs the class explains the plan. Then it’s aprons on and on to the pasta: dough kneaded by hand from scratch, rolled out and shaped with traditional Neapolitan tools, every step demonstrated before you do it.

Part two is the tiramisù, from the cream to the assembly, with a tasting of limoncello or meloncello (the melon version), or espresso and amaro. You can ask questions in Italian, English, Spanish or French. Water is unlimited throughout. The group is capped at sixteen people, and everyone actually cooks rather than just watching.

At the end you sit down and eat your own pasta and tiramisù, which make a proper lunch or dinner. You get a diploma and the recipes in digital form, so you can make them again at home. The hands-on part takes about two and a half hours; with the welcome and the meal it comes to three. Free luggage storage is available if you arrive with a suitcase.
1032625.perChi: Ideal for couples, families and solo travellers who want to meet people: you cook side by side and eat together. Also great on your arrival or departure day, thanks to the luggage storage. Not suitable for coeliacs, people with food allergies or diabetics. Babies under one aren’t allowed; older children tend to love the tiramisù part most.
1032625.consiglio: Come hungry, because what you cook is a full meal. Mention any intolerances when you book so they can set up your station. The restaurant is near the port and the Teatro San Carlo: before or after, take in the Galleria Umberto, Palazzo Reale and Piazza del Plebiscito, all a few minutes’ walk away.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: Explanations are in Italian and English, and the person running the class also speaks Spanish and French. The group is small, so it’s easy to ask for a step to be repeated. It runs every day except Sunday and lasts about three hours.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: A welcome glass of prosecco or a soft drink, a Neapolitan starter, all the ingredients and tools, an apron to use, water, a tasting of limoncello or meloncello or coffee and amaro, the meal with the dishes you’ve made, the diploma with digital recipes, and luggage storage. Transport and tips aren’t included.

faq.q: Is it suitable for people with intolerances?
faq.a: Not for coeliacs or anyone with serious food allergies: you work with flour, eggs, dairy and coffee in a shared space. The tiramisù isn’t recommended for diabetics. For other needs, it’s best to mention them when booking. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

1098790.intro: A day on a boat between Procida and Ischia, with the skipper choosing the route according to the sea. You leave Molo Beverello by hydrofoil, forty minutes to Procida, and board the boat there. From then on it’s all sea: the Corricella with its coloured houses, the volcanic coast of Ischia, bays to stop and swim in, and a lunch prepared on board, with sparkling wine and soft drinks. You don’t go ashore on Ischia; you see it from the water.
cosaSiFa: Meet at Molo Beverello in Naples. The hydrofoil to Procida is included and takes forty minutes. On arrival you board the boat with the skipper and start by circling the island: Marina Corricella, the fishermen’s houses, the little coves. Then you head for Ischia, sailing along its coast without landing, past volcanic cliffs and hidden inlets.

Along the way there are swim stops in clear water, with the boat anchored in a bay. At some point lunch is served: fresella (a crunchy Neapolitan rusk topped with tomatoes), pasta and fruit prepared on board, with spumante, prosecco or champagne and soft drinks included. In the afternoon you return to Procida, and from there the hydrofoil takes you back to Molo Beverello, another forty minutes. Seven hours in total.
1098790.perChi: For anyone who wants a real day at sea, not a ferry crossing: swims, lunch with wet feet and the islands seen from the water. Works well solo or as a couple, as the group is small. Not for anyone prone to seasickness: the route changes with the waves and the boat moves. Under-18s must be accompanied.
1098790.consiglio: Wear your swimsuit and bring a towel, sunscreen and a camera: there are no towels on board. No heels. If the sea is rough, the skipper changes course to find sheltered bays: that’s not a flaw, it’s the whole point of going on a small boat. Hotel transfers can be requested separately.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: Seven hours, from Molo Beverello and back to the same spot. The return hydrofoil to Procida is included, forty minutes each way; you board the boat with the skipper in Procida. Hotel pickup isn’t included but can be arranged separately for a fee.

faq.q: What do we eat and what’s included?
faq.a: An Italian lunch prepared on board with fresella, pasta and fruit; spumante, prosecco or champagne and soft drinks. The swim stops and a professional skipper are included. Bring your own towels and beach gear.

faq.q: Do we land on Ischia? What languages does the skipper speak?
faq.a: No, you sail along Ischia’s coast without going ashore; in Procida you do stop, to switch from the hydrofoil to the boat. The skipper speaks English, Italian and Spanish. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure.

1142689.intro: Three hours in a Neapolitan kitchen with a professional chef, learning two fresh pastas from scratch, fettuccine and ricotta-filled ravioli, plus a hand-whipped tiramisù. You start with eggs and flour, make a sauce with San Marzano DOP tomatoes, and at the end sit down to eat what you’ve made, with a glass of wine or a beer. No experience needed; you leave with the recipes and a diploma.
cosaSiFa: You arrive, put on an apron and hat, and start with a Neapolitan starter while the chef explains the family recipe. Then you knead: fresh eggs and flour, rolling the dough until it’s smooth and elastic, then cutting the fettuccine. Meanwhile the sauce is made with San Marzano tomatoes.

Second pasta, the ravioli: everyone rolls out their sheet, fills it with fresh ricotta and spices and seals their own by hand, one by one. Then it’s on to the tiramisù, with the mascarpone cream worked to the right consistency, the savoiardi (ladyfingers) dipped in coffee, the layers built up slowly and cocoa on top.

At the end everyone sits down with the chef and the other participants: fettuccine Alfredo, ravioli with tomato sauce and the tiramisù, with your chosen drink and unlimited water, finishing with a limoncello. Before you leave you get the recipes via a QR code on your personalised diploma, and a number to call for help when you try it at home.
1142689.perChi: For anyone who has never made pasta at home and wants to go back with two real techniques, and for couples and families: it suits all ages, and under-18s must be accompanied by an adult. Classes run in Italian, English, French and Spanish. Less suited to anyone who just wants to eat without getting behind the counter.
1142689.consiglio: Wear comfortable clothes without bulky sleeves; your hands will be in the flour. Come hungry: you eat everything you make, starter included. Keep the diploma, as the QR code with the recipes really comes in handy when you want to make the ravioli again at home.

faq.q: How long is it and do I need to know how to cook?
faq.a: Three hours, including the cooking and lunch or dinner at the table with the other participants. No experience needed: the chef guides every step, from the dough to the tiramisù. Just bring comfortable clothes and an appetite.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The class with the chef, apron and hat, a Neapolitan starter, the ingredients for pasta, sauce and tiramisù, a drink of your choice (soft drink, beer or a glass of wine), mineral water, limoncello with dessert, the diploma with the recipe QR code and phone support afterwards.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: It runs in Italian, English, French or Spanish, depending on the date. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund. Suitable for all ages, with under-18s accompanied by an adult.

1242092.intro: The classic Amalfi Coast tour, but with no more than thirteen people on board. You leave from the central station area in an air-conditioned vehicle, with a tour leader who talks you through the road and a driver who knows every bend. The day lasts nine hours and takes in Amalfi, Positano and Sorrento in that order, with photo stops at the best spots. Water is included, lunch isn’t: you eat wherever you like during free time.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Garibaldi and set off: an hour and a half on the road to Amalfi, the longest stop of the day. You have two and a half hours free for the Cathedral of Sant’Andrea, the squares, the shops and a coffee by the harbour. If you like, you can go as far as the Grotta dello Smeraldo (the Emerald Grotto), but time it carefully so you don’t miss the minibus.

Three quarters of an hour of bends and you reach Positano, with an hour to walk down to the beach between the cliffside houses and boutiques. Then another forty-five minutes to Sorrento, for an hour among the lemon groves and the centre, with a taste of limoncello. After that you head back to Naples, an hour and a half to the starting point.
1242092.perChi: For anyone who wants to see all three towns in a day without crowds around them: thirteen people is a minibus, not a coach party. Good if you don’t have a car and don’t want to drive the coast road. The pace is brisk and in some places time flies, so it’s not the choice for anyone who wants to spend hours on the beach.
1242092.consiglio: Get to the meeting point a little early; the group is small and they won’t wait long. Amalfi is the longest stop, so that’s where to have a leisurely lunch. Positano is shorter: take your photo from above and head straight down. Book ahead, as places sell out.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long is it?
faq.a: The meeting point is Piazza Garibaldi, in front of the central station, and that’s where you return at the end of the day. Nine hours in all: three stops in the towns and about four and a half hours on the road, going out, between towns and coming back.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The tour leader speaks English and Spanish; dates with Italian are shown when you book. The group is limited to thirteen participants, so you can hear well and ask questions easily. Bottled water is included.

faq.q: Is lunch included? Can I cancel?
faq.a: No, lunch isn’t included: you eat during free time, and the longest stop is in Amalfi. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, and you can book now and pay later, so if you change your mind you lose nothing.

1289947.intro: The Fontanelle Cemetery is an ossuary of about three thousand square metres carved into the tuff (soft volcanic rock) of the hillside, in the Rione Sanità. This is where the cult of the anime pezzentelle, the ‘poor souls’, was born: Neapolitans would adopt a nameless skull and pray to it, and faith blended with folklore. A forty-minute guided visit, in Italian, along the three naves, ticket included. The fee goes to the neighbourhood cooperative that runs the site.
cosaSiFa: You show up at the entrance on Via Fontanelle and go in with the guide. The route runs through the three great galleries: the Nave of the Priests, the Nave of the Plague Victims and the Nave of the Pezzentelli, all carved into the tuff quarry 74 metres above sea level.

Walking among the skulls and bones, the guide explains how the ossuary came about and how the cult of the anime pezzentelle began, with skulls adopted by the people of the neighbourhood. Then the legends: the Captain’s Skull, Concetta’s «sweating head» and the stories still going round the neighbourhood.

Forty minutes later you’re out, with the historical and architectural background explained along the way. If you select the option with the audio guide app, you get that too. The guides were born and raised in the neighbourhood, and the ticket supports a cooperative recognised as a model social enterprise.
1289947.perChi: For anyone who wants to understand how Neapolitans relate to death, not just see a strange place. Good if you’re short on time: forty minutes, easy to combine with the rest of the Sanità. With children it depends on how sensitive they are; these are real skulls. The whole route is inside the galleries.
1289947.consiglio: Bring a sweatshirt: it’s cool in the quarry all year round. Pair it with the rest of the Rione Sanità, with Palazzo dello Spagnolo and the Catacombs of San Gennaro, so the morning hangs together. Arrive a few minutes before your slot. Book in good time, as it often sells out.

faq.q: How long is it and what language is it in?
faq.a: Forty minutes, with a guide in Italian. If you select the option with the audio guide app, it’s included in the ticket.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The entry ticket and the guided visit along the three naves. The fee supports the Rione Sanità cooperative that runs the site and the project to revive the neighbourhood.

faq.q: Where is it and can I cancel?
faq.a: On Via Fontanelle, in the Rione Sanità. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

1308037.intro: A 75–90-minute boat trip around the bay, leaving from Santa Lucia at the foot of Castel dell’Ovo. You sail out of the little harbour and see Naples the way people arriving by sea used to: Vesuvius in the background, the castle, then the Posillipo coast with its villas and finally Nisida, the volcanic islet. On board a guide gives live commentary in Italian and English; there’s a covered deck and an open but shaded one, with 360-degree views.
cosaSiFa: Show up at the Santa Lucia quay, in the Borgo Marinari, a quarter of an hour before departure for boarding. The boats carry up to sixty people and have life jackets and safety equipment. Sit wherever you like: under the covered deck or outside in the shade, with a clear view across the whole bay.

As soon as you leave the harbour the skyline opens up: Vesuvius on one side, Castel dell’Ovo seemingly floating on the other. You sail west along the Posillipo coast, with villas perched on the cliffs, as far as Nisida. The guide tells the story of the places, from the Greek colonists to today, with live commentary in Italian and English.

Then you head back to the same spot. 75–90 minutes in all. There are two departures a day, one in the morning and one in the afternoon, from April to November. Boats go out even in uncertain weather; if the sea isn’t safe the trip is cancelled and you’re refunded automatically.
1308037.perChi: It’s the easiest way to see Naples from the sea: no effort, an hour and a quarter sitting down. Good for families with children, couples and anyone short on time. Not recommended for anyone prone to seasickness or for pregnant women. If you want to swim, look for a different trip: this is a sightseeing cruise.
1308037.consiglio: The afternoon departure has the best light on Posillipo. Bring water and a hat: even in the shade, it’s hot in summer. The boarding point is five minutes’ walk from Piazza del Plebiscito, so combine it with the seafront or a stroll around the Borgo Marinari before you board.

faq.q: Where does it leave from and how long is it?
faq.a: It leaves from and returns to the Santa Lucia quay, in the Borgo Marinari, next to Castel dell’Ovo and a few minutes’ walk from Piazza del Plebiscito. It lasts 75 to 90 minutes. You need to be there 15 minutes early for boarding.

faq.q: What’s included and what isn’t?
faq.a: The boat trip, the guide’s live commentary in Italian and English, the covered deck and the shaded outdoor deck, life jackets and safety equipment. Food and drinks, hotel pickup and parking aren’t included.

faq.q: What if the weather’s bad?
faq.a: The cruise runs in most weather conditions. If it’s cancelled because the sea isn’t safe, you get a full automatic refund. Either way, you can cancel for free up to 24 hours before.

1320588.intro: Herculaneum is smaller than Pompeii and better preserved: here the mud of AD 79 sealed in upper floors, wood and frescoes. This tour covers it in half a day, leaving Piazza Garibaldi in an air-conditioned minivan, going in with priority tickets and spending two hours with a licensed guide dedicated to your group. At the end the minivan brings you back to the starting point. The afternoon is yours.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Garibaldi, in front of a hotel next to the station, and get into the minivan. The drive to Herculaneum is short and scenic, with Vesuvius ahead. At the Archaeological Park you meet the guide, who works only with your group, and go in with priority access, skipping the ticket office queue.

The walking visit lasts two hours: everyday Roman life, houses with their upper floors still standing, carbonised materials, mosaics, and the story of the eruption that buried the town. When the tour ends, the minivan takes the group back to Naples, to the same spot you left from. About three hours in all.
1320588.perChi: For anyone who wants to see one of the Vesuvian sites properly and calmly without giving up a whole day, and for those who prefer a guide just for their own group. The tour is in English. Less suited to anyone hoping to combine Pompeii and Herculaneum in one trip: this one visits Herculaneum only.
1320588.consiglio: Bring a camera or a fully charged phone: the interiors of the houses are worth it. Food and drinks aren’t included, so have breakfast first and bring a bottle of water. If you want to carry on to Vesuvius afterwards, ask the guide about connections from Ercolano.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About three hours, two of them on the guided visit inside the park. The meeting point is Piazza Garibaldi, in front of a hotel next to the central station, and the minivan brings you back there at the end.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: Return transport in an air-conditioned minivan, skip-the-line entry tickets for Herculaneum with priority access and the two-hour private guided visit. Food and drinks aren’t included.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later. Dates often sell out, so it’s best to book a few days ahead.

101354P2.intro: An hour in the saddle on the old lava trails of Vesuvius, at a walking pace, with a guide who talks you through the eruptions and the civilisations the volcano left its mark on. The horses follow ancient tracks between vineyards growing on volcanic soil, and every bend opens up a view of the bay. This isn’t a ride for anyone who wants to gallop: it’s about spending time with the animals and taking in the scenery. Two hours in total, with helmet, water and a shuttle from Pompei Scavi included.
cosaSiFa: You set off from Pompei Scavi on the shuttle that climbs to the starting point on the slopes of the volcano. There you’re matched with your horse, put on a helmet and get the basic instructions. The pace stays at a walk the whole way: if you’re after speed you’ll be disappointed, if you want to look around you’re in the right place.

The route follows the old lava trails, through vineyards and open stretches with views over the bay and the countryside below. The guide, in English or Spanish, explains how the eruptions shaped the landscape and what happened to the towns at the foot of the volcano. There are stops for photos, and plenty of viewpoints to choose from.

The ride itself lasts about an hour; with the shuttle, getting ready and heading back, it comes to two hours. Groups are capped at 10 people and water is included. You finish where you started, and the shuttle takes you back to Pompei Scavi.
101354P2.perChi: For anyone who wants to see Vesuvius without hiking up to the crater, and for animal lovers: the pace is slow and the focus is on the landscape. Good for families with older kids and for couples. Not for adrenaline seekers or anyone who wants to gallop; the guide speaks English or Spanish, not Italian.
101354P2.consiglio: Long trousers and closed shoes, no sandals: you need them in the saddle and on the lava. Bring a hat and sunscreen, as there’s little shade on the volcano. Pair it with the ruins of Pompeii, since the shuttle leaves from there: ruins in the morning, horses in the afternoon, or the other way round. Book early in the warmer months, as groups are ten people at most.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it start?
faq.a: About 2 hours in total, around one of them in the saddle. You start from Pompei Scavi with the included shuttle, which drives up the slopes of Vesuvius and brings you back at the end. Groups are capped at 10 people.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The helmet, water, the shuttle to and from Pompei Scavi, the horse and the guide who leads the group along the lava trails. Nothing else is included: bring what you need for the sun and to be comfortable in the saddle.

faq.q: Do we gallop? What language does the guide speak?
faq.a: No. The ride is at a walk, designed for spending time with the horses and enjoying the view, not for going fast. The guide speaks English and Spanish. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start.

101354P7.intro: Two hours inside the ruins with an expert guide and a group of no more than twenty. The skip-the-line ticket is included, and you meet at the Porta Marina Superiore entrance. You’ll see theatres, temples and bath complexes, with the guide explaining how everyday Roman life worked and pointing out corners you’d walk straight past on your own. If you’re staying in Naples, you can add return transport.
cosaSiFa: Meet ten minutes early at the Porta Marina Superiore entrance, where the guide waits with a green sign. If you’ve chosen the option with transport, a minivan picks you up in Naples in the morning from the designated pickup point. With tickets already in hand, you walk straight in, no ticket office and no queues.

The guided walk lasts two hours and takes you through the city buried in AD 79: the streets, theatres, temples, bath complexes and houses, with the guide describing the daily life of the people who lived there. It’s in English. At the end you leave by the same entrance; if you have transport, the minivan takes you back to Naples.
101354P7.perChi: For anyone getting to Pompeii under their own steam, by train or car, who just wants the guided visit without a full-day package. Suitable for all fitness levels, and pushchairs are allowed. The guide speaks English: if you don’t follow it well, pick a different tour. Private groups can ask for the dedicated option.
101354P7.consiglio: Arrive ten minutes early, as the group leaves on time. Bring water, a hat and closed shoes: the streets are stone and shade is scarce. After booking you’ll get an automatic email with all the instructions, so read it. If you choose transport from Naples, the morning pickup only runs from the designated point.

faq.q: How long is it and where do we meet?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts two hours. You meet outside the Porta Marina Superiore entrance, where the guide holds a green sign, ten minutes before the start time. If you choose the option with transport, you’re picked up in Naples in the morning from the designated pickup point.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Groups are limited to twenty people, so you can follow along and ask questions without shouting. There’s also a private option if you want a visit just for yourselves.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: The skip-the-line ticket for the ruins and the two-hour guided visit. Transport from Naples is only included in the dedicated option. Tips aren’t included. Pushchairs and wheelchairs are allowed. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before the start.

103374P5.intro: Two and a half hours combining the two things people do most in Naples: eating and looking around. You start from Piazza Bellini and at each stop you taste a different dish, while in between the guide, in English, takes you to the places in the old town worth seeing. Groups of up to 15, tastings included. It’s the tour for anyone with just one afternoon who doesn’t want to choose between the monument and the sandwich.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bellini, then walk through the old town. The stops are chosen to bring a different flavour to the counter each time: you taste standing up, listen to the explanation and move on. The programme doesn’t list the dishes one by one, but the idea is Neapolitan street food: the specialities people here eat every day.

Between tastings the route passes the main sights of the centre, and the guide talks about them the way a local friend would: what they are, why they matter, what’s round the corner. The pace is relaxed and the distances short, because in the old town everything is close together.
Two and a half hours in all, in English, with a maximum of 15 people. You finish with a full stomach and a clear idea of where to go back to on your own in the following days.
103374P5.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants a single tour covering both the food and the sights of the centre, without going too deep into either. Good for first-timers and groups. Less suited to anyone who doesn’t follow English well or who wants a proper art tour.
103374P5.consiglio: Come hungry and wear comfortable shoes: you eat standing up and walk on basalt paving stones. Piazza Bellini is just behind Via dei Tribunali, so before or after the tour you can stretch your legs to the Duomo or San Gregorio Armeno. Weekend slots fill up, so book ahead.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long is it?
faq.a: You meet in Piazza Bellini, in the old town, and walk for about two and a half hours between food stops and sights. Groups are capped at 15 people.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The tastings at each stop and the guide. Every stop offers a different speciality, so by the end the tastings add up to a meal. Any extra food or drinks are paid separately.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund; after that the ticket is non-refundable. It’s worth mentioning any dietary needs when you book.

104566P11.intro: Two and a half hours in the lanes of the old town with an English-speaking guide who knows where Neapolitans stop to eat standing up. You taste fresh buffalo mozzarella, pizza fritta (deep-fried pizza), a slice of margherita, and finish with a small glass of limoncello. Between bites, the guide shares the history and stories of one of the oldest cities in Italy. Groups of up to 15, starting from Piazza Bellini.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bellini. From there you head into the lanes of the ancient centre and start with buffalo mozzarella, eaten fresh as it should be. Next comes pizza fritta, which people here eat on the move, and a slice of margherita, the oven-baked chapter of the same story.

At every stop the guide explains what you’re eating and tells you about the history of the city and the neighbourhoods you walk through. The last stop is limoncello, a small glass to round things off. It’s two and a half hours of slow walking with frequent stops. The organisers are clear about it: come on an empty stomach.
Groups are capped at 15 people and the tour is in English. The pace is set by the lanes: narrow streets, short stops, lots of people around, especially at weekends and at mealtimes.
104566P11.perChi: For first-timers who want to cover the basics of Neapolitan street food in one afternoon without hunting down the places themselves. Good for groups of friends and solo travellers, since the group is small. Less suited to anyone who doesn’t follow English: the guide only speaks that language.
104566P11.consiglio: Go easy on breakfast and skip lunch: the tastings are a proper meal. Wear comfortable shoes for the paving stones. Piazza Bellini is a stone’s throw from Via dei Tribunali and San Gregorio Armeno, so there’s plenty to walk to before or after. Book ahead for bank holidays and weekends.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long is it?
faq.a: You start from Piazza Bellini, in the old town, and walk for about two and a half hours through the lanes. It’s on foot at a gentle pace, with frequent stops to eat and listen to the guide.

faq.q: What do we eat and what’s included?
faq.a: The tastings at every stop are included in the ticket: buffalo mozzarella, pizza fritta, a slice of margherita and a small glass of limoncello, plus the guide. Come hungry, as the tastings add up to a meal.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Groups are capped at 15 people. You can cancel for free up to 24 hours before the start for a full refund; after that the ticket is non-refundable.

116146P37.intro: The classic tour of the peninsula in one day, in an air-conditioned vehicle with at most twenty seats and a driver who doubles as your host along the way. You stop at the viewpoint over Positano, spend an hour and a half in Sorrento with a limoncello tasting, and finish with two hours in Pompeii, where you can explore on your own or with a licensed guide if you choose that option. Pickup is at the Stazione Marittima or other points in the city.
cosaSiFa: You leave Naples from the cruise terminal or another agreed point and head by minivan towards the coast. The first stop is the viewpoint over Positano: a short stop to look down on the coloured houses tumbling towards the sea and take a few photos, without going down into the village.

Then Sorrento, with an hour and a half to yourself. Piazza Tasso, Corso Italia with its shops, the cloister of San Francesco and the view over the bay from the terraces. The limoncello tasting included in the price happens here too. Lunch isn’t included: everyone sorts themselves out, with a meeting time set by the driver.

In the afternoon, two hours in Pompeii. The entry ticket isn’t included, and there’s only a guide inside the ruins if you book that option; otherwise you visit at your own pace. The order of the stops may change depending on traffic or the group’s preferences. At the end you head back to Naples.
116146P37.perChi: For anyone who wants to see a lot in a short time in a small vehicle without worrying about timetables, especially cruise passengers and families: the tour is wheelchair accessible with advance notice, pushchairs are allowed and child seats are available. Less suited to anyone wanting an in-depth visit to Pompeii without paying for the guide option.
116146P37.consiglio: Consider the option with a guide at Pompeii: without one, two hours in the ruins with no explanations don’t give you much. Buy your ticket for the ruins in advance so you don’t lose time. In Sorrento, an hour and a half is enough for a walk or a quick lunch, not both at a relaxed pace.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About eight hours. Pickup is available at the Stazione Marittima, the Naples cruise terminal, or at other points in the city; for cruise passengers departure is at 8am, depending on the ship’s schedule. The port of Salerno is only for cruise passengers.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The air-conditioned minivan with an English-speaking driver-host and commentary on board, pickup, a bottle of water each and the limoncello tasting in Sorrento. Not included: the Pompeii ticket, a guide inside the ruins unless you choose that option, lunch and extra activities.

faq.q: Can I cancel? Is there a minimum number of people?
faq.a: Yes, cancel at least 24 hours before departure for a full refund. The tour needs a minimum number of participants: if it isn’t reached 24 hours before, you can move to another date or reschedule. Available languages are Italian and English.

162012P20.intro: A three-hour class in a venue on Via delle Zite to make fresh egg pasta, ravioli and fettuccine, and a tiramisù from start to finish. You also prepare two sauces, a creamy tomato one and a San Marzano with fresh basil, then sit down to eat what you’ve made with a drink. You go home with the recipes and a personalised diploma.
cosaSiFa: You start with dessert: the tiramisù has to be made first because it needs to rest. Cream, biscuits dipped in coffee, layers and cocoa, with the chef correcting as you go. Meanwhile he explains how handmade pasta is a family affair in southern Italy and what changes with seasonal ingredients.

Then the egg pasta. You knead, roll out and cut the fettuccine, then seal the ravioli using traditional techniques. Meanwhile the two sauces come together: the creamy tomato one and the one with San Marzano tomatoes and fresh basil, to dress what you’ve just made.

Once everything’s cooked, you all sit down and eat: ravioli, fettuccine with the two sauces and, to finish, the tiramisù, with a drink. You leave with a personalised diploma and the written recipes, so you can make it all again at home without guessing the quantities.
162012P20.perChi: For anyone who wants to go home actually knowing how to make something, not just having watched. Works for couples, groups of friends and families; groups can reach 25 people, so don’t expect a private lesson. Three hours standing with your hands in the dough: if you’re short on time or don’t fancy the counter, a shorter tour may suit you better.
162012P20.consiglio: Do it at lunch or dinner time and don’t eat beforehand: pasta with two sauces plus tiramisù is filling. Wear clothes that can get floury. Via delle Zite is a fifteen-minute walk from the central station and the Duomo, handy if you’re arriving by train. Book a few days ahead.

faq.q: What do we make and what’s included?
faq.a: Fresh egg pasta in two shapes, ravioli and fettuccine, two sauces and a tiramisù. You eat everything you make at the end of the class, with a drink. The personalised diploma and recipes are included. It lasts about three hours.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian; you choose the language when booking. Groups can be up to 25 people, so the chef moves between the stations explaining as he goes.

faq.q: Can I cancel and where do we meet?
faq.a: Free cancellation up to 24 hours before the start. The meeting point is on Via delle Zite, between the central station and the old town.

162012P38.intro: A three-hour class near Via Duomo where you make the two things everyone wants to learn in Naples: pizza and tiramisù. You start from the flour, knead by hand, stretch the dough and bake it in a traditional oven; then you move on to dessert, layer by layer. You eat what you’ve made, with a starter and a drink included, and go home with the written recipes.
cosaSiFa: You start with the pizza. The chef shows how Neapolitan dough is made from the basic ingredients, then everyone works their own ball of dough: kneading, stretching it by hand, adding the toppings. It’s baked in the traditional oven, and what comes out is your pizza, to eat there and then with the included starter and drink.

The second part is the tiramisù, followed step by step: you make the cream, dip the biscuits, build the layers. At the end everyone has their own dessert. You get the pizza and tiramisù recipes to make them again at home. The class runs in English, Spanish, French or Italian depending on your booking, and lasts about three hours.
162012P38.perChi: Good for couples, groups of friends and families with children who want to get their hands dirty. Groups can reach thirty people, so don’t expect a private lesson: if you want more attention, look for a smaller class. It’s three hours on your feet, so better not to schedule it after a full day of walking.
162012P38.consiglio: Treat it as a meal: you eat a starter, pizza and tiramisù, so skip lunch beforehand. Wear clothes that can get floury. The kitchen is near Via Duomo: beforehand you can see the Duomo and the Chapel of San Gennaro, or wander down San Gregorio Armeno, a few minutes away.

faq.q: What do we make and what do we eat?
faq.a: You make a Neapolitan pizza, from the dough to baking it in a traditional oven, and a tiramisù. You eat what you’ve made, with a starter and a drink included. At the end of the class you get the recipes to make it all again at home.

faq.q: What languages is the class in and how long is it?
faq.a: The class lasts three hours and runs in English, Spanish, French or Italian: you choose the language when booking. Groups can be up to thirty participants, led by a local chef.

faq.q: Where is it and can I cancel?
faq.a: The kitchen is in the Via Duomo area, in the old town of Naples; the exact address comes with your confirmation. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the class starts.

162012P56.intro: Three hours in the kitchen with a local chef on Via delle Zite, making two pastas and a dessert: fettuccine with Alfredo sauce, the butter and Parmigiano one, ricotta-filled ravioli with San Marzano tomato sauce, and tiramisù. You start from the ingredients, fresh ricotta and aged Parmigiano in hand, and finish at the table eating what you’ve made. There’s a diploma at the end.
cosaSiFa: The class opens with an introduction to the ingredients: fresh ricotta, aged Parmigiano, eggs and flour. It helps you understand why pasta turns out well or badly before you even touch it. Then you knead, roll out the sheet and cut the fettuccine, while the chef moves between the stations and straightens out anyone going off course.

The second pasta is ravioli: you make the ricotta filling, seal them one by one and put the San Marzano tomato sauce on. For the fettuccine you make the Alfredo sauce, with butter and Parmigiano. Meanwhile the tiramisù is assembled, as it needs its time in the fridge.

At the end you all eat together at the tables, with the chef sharing local stories and tips to take home. The tiramisù rounds it off. You leave with a certificate of participation. The class is designed for all levels, so nobody gets left behind, not even people who have never kneaded dough.
162012P56.perChi: For families, couples and groups of friends, even large ones: groups go up to thirty people, so it’s the right choice if there are lots of you and you want to stay together.
