Good for anyone who has never made pasta. If you’d rather have an intimate class with the chef all to yourself, look at the options with ten places.
162012P56.consiglio: Don’t eat beforehand: three hours later you leave with two pastas and a dessert inside you. Via delle Zite is right in the old town: beforehand, a walk along the decumani (the ancient Roman streets) and San Gregorio Armeno, a few minutes away on foot, fits in nicely. Comfortable clothes and short sleeves, as you roll out the pasta with your arms.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: The chef speaks Italian, English, Spanish and French; you choose the language when booking. The class lasts three hours and takes place on Via delle Zite, in the old town of Naples. Groups can be up to thirty people.

faq.q: What do we make and what do we eat?
faq.a: Fettuccine with butter and Parmigiano Alfredo sauce, ricotta ravioli with San Marzano tomato sauce, and tiramisù. You eat everything you make at the end of the class, sitting together. The two sauces and the certificate of participation are included.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. The class suits all levels, so no cooking experience is needed: just turn up in comfortable clothes, ready to get your hands dirty.

162012P8.intro: Two hours on foot, downhill, from the Vomero to the centre, by way of the Petraio: the pedestrian stairway that winds down between houses, vegetable gardens and terraces, and that most tourists don’t even know exists. You go up by funicular, included in the ticket, and come down at an easy pace, with the bay, Capri and Vesuvius in front of you at several points. Groups of up to fifteen, with a local guide.
cosaSiFa: You meet in the Vomero, the well-to-do neighbourhood on the hill: elegant buildings, wide streets, a different Naples from the one in the lanes below. The funicular is included in the ticket and covers the uphill part. From here you look down on the city and the guide explains what you’re seeing, from the port to Vesuvius.

Then you join the Petraio and start down: steps, bends, glimpses of the sea between buildings, washing hung out to dry. This is the photogenic part of the walk, and the guide points out the spots to stop. As you descend, the houses and the people change, from grand apartment blocks to working-class streets.

You reach the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), with their grid of lanes and stairs where the city feels most itself, and finish in the centre, out on the street, with the rest of the day ahead of you. The stories along the way are about the city and the people who live in it, not just the monuments, and that’s what sets it apart from a classic tour.
162012P8.perChi: For anyone who loves walking and taking photos, and who wants to see Naples from an angle you don’t get from the lanes. The descent is long and all steps: bad knees and pushchairs won’t enjoy it. Good for couples, friends and solo travellers; with fifteen people at most, it’s easy to stay together.
162012P8.consiglio: Shoes with good grip and a bottle of water: there’s a lot of descending. The best light over the bay is in the morning or late afternoon. Before you start, it’s worth going up to Castel Sant’Elmo or the Certosa di San Martino, both in the Vomero with the same view; afterwards, the Quartieri Spagnoli and Via Toledo are right there.

faq.q: How much walking is there and how long is it?
faq.a: The tour lasts about two hours, almost all on foot and downhill, from the Vomero to the centre via the Petraio, a pedestrian stairway. You go up by funicular, included in the ticket. You need comfortable shoes and legs in decent shape.

faq.q: What languages is it available in?
faq.a: Italian, English, Spanish and French; you choose the language when booking. Groups are up to fifteen people, with a local guide who stays with you the whole way and shares stories and curiosities about the neighbourhoods you pass through.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: The local guide and the funicular are included. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. Available start times are shown when you book, depending on the date you choose.

162012P9.intro: Two hours on foot between the old town and the Pignasecca market, with six stops to eat: you open with a spritz and a board of cured meats and mozzarella, continue with tarallo, pizza a portafoglio and a cuoppo of fried fish, then a meatball in ragù, and finish with sfogliatella or gelato and a limoncello or a coffee. The guide tells stories and legends of the neighbourhood between bites.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Carità, a step from the Pignasecca. You start with a spritz and a board of cured meats and mozzarella to break the ice, while the guide explains how the market works and where the things you’re about to eat come from, in places where Neapolitans actually go.

Then you walk and eat: a tarallo, a folded pizza a portafoglio to hold in your hand, and the cuoppo, a paper cone of fried fish. The fifth stop is a meatball slow-cooked in ragù. You’re among the market stalls and eateries, with the guide’s stories and tips between one bite and the next.

You finish with dessert: sfogliatella (the shell-shaped pastry) or artisan gelato, your choice, with a limoncello or an espresso. There’s a vegetarian option, to be requested when booking. About two hours in all, six tastings and dessert.
162012P9.perChi: For anyone who wants to eat the way people eat here, standing up and without sitting down in a restaurant. Good for couples and groups of friends, and for anyone short on time: two hours and you’ve had a full meal. Works with children if they eat everything. If you have allergies or intolerances, say so in advance; there’s a vegetarian version.
162012P9.consiglio: Come on an empty stomach, really: six stops with pizza, fried food and a meatball make a big lunch. Comfortable shoes and no bulky bags, as it’s a tight squeeze between the market stalls. Piazza Carità is on Via Toledo: afterwards, the Galleria Umberto and Piazza del Plebiscito are ten minutes downhill.

faq.q: What do we eat on the tour?
faq.a: A spritz with a board of cured meats and mozzarella, a tarallo, a pizza a portafoglio, a cuoppo of fried fish, a meatball in ragù and a dessert, either sfogliatella or gelato, with limoncello or coffee. A vegetarian option is available.

faq.q: What language is it in and how long is it?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian. It lasts about two hours, in groups of up to fifteen people.

faq.q: Where does it start and can I cancel?
faq.a: Meet in Piazza Carità, at the start of the Pignasecca. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

165824P1.intro: A three-hour walk between the Galleria Umberto I and the Quartieri Spagnoli, with six tastings and three drinks along the way. The theme is the food of Naples when it was the capital of a kingdom: dishes once served at court that are still eaten in the lanes today. You taste pasta, mop up the sauce with bread, move on to pizza margherita and finish with a sfogliatella. Small group, twelve people at most, with an English-speaking guide.
cosaSiFa: You start from the Galleria Umberto I, a few steps from Via Toledo. The first stops set the scene: what the kings and queens of Naples ate and how those dishes made their way onto everyone’s table. You walk and stop at places in the centre, each for a different tasting, while the guide tells the story.

Then you head up into the Quartieri Spagnoli, where the guide shares the neighbourhood’s legends and traditions between stops. This is where the heartier part comes: a plate of Neapolitan-style pasta, with bread for the scarpetta, mopping up every last drop of sauce, and a pizza margherita made the way it is here.

The finale is sweet, with a sfogliatella in a local café. Six tastings and three drinks in all, spread over the three hours, so it’s best to arrive hungry and skip the previous meal. At the end you’re still in the centre, a few minutes from Via Toledo and Piazza del Plebiscito.
165824P1.perChi: Made for anyone who wants to eat Neapolitan food without hunting for places on their own and prefers a small group, twelve people at most. The guide only speaks English: if you don’t follow it well, you’ll miss out on the stories. You walk for three hours, including uphill in the Quartieri; a pushchair can be awkward. Not for anyone in a hurry.
165824P1.consiglio: Book it for lunch or dinner time and arrive on an empty stomach: six tastings are a full meal. Comfortable shoes, because the Quartieri Spagnoli are uphill. Before or after, take a look around the Galleria Umberto I and Piazza del Plebiscito, right next door.

faq.q: How long is it and how many tastings are there?
faq.a: The tour lasts three hours and includes six tastings and three drinks, from pasta to pizza margherita to sfogliatella. You walk between the centre and the Quartieri Spagnoli, stopping at different places. Groups are limited to twelve people.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. No other languages are offered, so only book it if you can comfortably follow three hours of explanations in English. The food part, of course, needs no translation.

faq.q: Where’s the meeting point and how do I cancel?
faq.a: You meet at the Galleria Umberto I, in the centre of Naples, near Via Toledo and Piazza del Plebiscito; the exact details come with your confirmation. You can cancel for free up to 24 hours before the start.

165824P2.intro: Three and a half hours in the old town eating pizza in all its forms: at least six kinds, from the classic to the fried, in local pizzerias chosen by an English-speaking guide. Between tastings you walk the UNESCO stretch between Port’Alba and the Decumani, step into a church and drink a spritz in the roof garden of a 15th-century palazzo. Small group, twelve people at most.
cosaSiFa: You start from Port’Alba, the 1625 gate linking Piazza Dante to the street of booksellers. The first stop is at a place in the old town that has been going for over fifty years, for pizza with scarola (escarole), olives and walnuts: Neapolitan peasant cooking, twenty minutes. Then Piazza del Gesù, with the story of the façade of the Gesù Nuovo and its wartime miracle.

Second stop, the montanara: fried dough, tomato and cheese, the street food that legend says King Ferdinand of Bourbon loved. Another twenty minutes of tasting and off you go again. Forty minutes later you’re inside a palazzo from 1412, once the embassy of the Republic of Venice, with a spritz in the roof garden among art and history.

You carry on towards Piazzetta Nilo and the Decumani with more pizzas, ending with a small dessert. Stops and tastings may change depending on the day and the season, but the total is always at least six different pizzas, from the classics to more modern ones like the fried version. You finish with a full stomach and no need for dinner.
165824P2.perChi: For anyone who wants to understand pizza in Naples beyond the margherita, and who’d rather be guided by a local than pick places at random. The guide only speaks English. Vegetarian and gluten-free diets can be accommodated if you mention them when booking; not suitable for anyone with serious food allergies. Under-fours join for free, without food.
165824P2.consiglio: Don’t have lunch beforehand: six pizzas is a lot, even by the slice. Arrive at the meeting point a quarter of an hour early; the confirmation email on your phone is all you need. The tour needs at least two participants to go ahead, so it’s a safer bet as a couple or with friends.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About three and a half hours. The meeting point is Port’Alba, the gate between Piazza Dante and the old town, in front of a bookshop: you’ll recognise the guide by the purple bag. Best to arrive fifteen minutes early so you can leave on time.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: At least six different pizzas in pizzerias in the centre, a classic spritz, a small dessert and the local English-speaking guide with tips about the city. Extra drinks, tips and transport to and from your hotel aren’t included.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children and can I cancel?
faq.a: Children under four join for free but without food; from four upwards they need a ticket with tastings included. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund.

18971P114.intro: A small-group pasta and tiramisù class, ten people at most, on Via Medina, a short walk from Piazza Municipio. You make two kinds of pasta by hand and a tiramisù with a chef who explains in Italian and English, and at the end you sit down to eat the results with a starter and a glass of wine. It lasts two to two and a half hours depending on the group size. Diploma, recipe book and luggage storage included.
cosaSiFa: You start with the tiramisù, which needs to rest while you work on everything else. The chef explains each step and has everyone do it, in Italian and English depending on who’s at the counter, from the mascarpone cream to the layers with biscuits and cocoa.

Then the fresh pasta: flour, eggs and hands. You knead, roll out and shape two different kinds of pasta, with the chef correcting thickness and cut. With ten people at most, there’s time for every question and to redo a step if it didn’t come out right.

At the end you sit round the table and eat what you’ve made, with the starter and a glass of wine; the tiramisù closes the meal. You leave with the diploma and the recipe book, and if you left your suitcases in storage, you pick them up on the way out.
18971P114.perChi: For anyone who has just checked out of their hotel or has a train to catch and wants to make good use of two hours: the luggage storage solves the problem. Small group, so it also works if you’re starting from zero in the kitchen. Couples, friends, families with older kids who want to get their hands dirty.
18971P114.consiglio: Book a time that coincides with lunch or dinner: after pasta and tiramisù you won’t eat anything else. Via Medina is five minutes from the Maschio Angioino and the Municipio metro stop, and handy from the port too. If you have luggage, use the storage and add a walk to Piazza del Plebiscito afterwards.

faq.q: How long is the class?
faq.a: Between two and two and a half hours, depending on the size of the group, which is ten people at most. The pace adapts to whoever is there.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The class with the chef, the ingredients for two kinds of pasta and for the tiramisù, a starter and a glass of wine at the table, the recipe book, the diploma and luggage storage.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian; the chef runs the class in Italian and English. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before. The meeting point is on Via Medina.

18971P130.intro: A two-and-a-half-hour class near Via Medina, designed for anyone who wants to make pizza at home for real: not in a wood-fired oven, but in the ruoto, the round baking tin Neapolitan families use, baked in a home oven. You knead, stretch and bake, then make tiramisù with mascarpone. Fifteen people at most, apron and digital recipe book included, and you can leave your suitcase.
cosaSiFa: You start with the dough: the chef explains the proportions and the technique, then everyone works their own. You stretch it into the ruoto and bake it in a home oven, so what you learn can be repeated without special equipment. Meanwhile you have the starter and something to drink; there’s an option with unlimited wine.

The second part is the tiramisù: mascarpone cream, biscuits and coffee, built up in layers. At the end everyone eats their own pizza and dessert, taking their time. The digital recipe book lets you make it all again at home. Allergies and intolerances must be mentioned when booking.
18971P130.perChi: Good for anyone who already cooks a bit and wants to take home a useful technique, and for families and couples looking for an afternoon without much walking. The group is small, fifteen at most. Handy on your last day too, before the train: you can leave your luggage. Not for anyone after wood-fired pizza.
18971P130.consiglio: Via Medina is a stone’s throw from the Maschio Angioino and Piazza Municipio: pair the class with a visit to the castle or the port. Arrive hungry, because between starter, pizza and tiramisù it’s a full meal. If you have an afternoon train, make use of the luggage storage.

faq.q: What’s included in the class?
faq.a: Apron, ingredients, starter and a drink, the digital recipe book and luggage storage. There’s an option with unlimited wine. You eat the pizza and tiramisù you make during the class, so it counts as a meal.

faq.q: How long is it and how many people take part?
faq.a: The class lasts about two and a half hours, in a group of up to fifteen people led by a local chef. It runs in Italian, English, Spanish or French, chosen when booking.

faq.q: Can I flag allergies and cancel?
faq.a: Yes: allergies and intolerances must be flagged when booking, as the operator requests. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the class starts.

18971P22.intro: The walking tour that brings the two Naples together: the grand one around Piazza del Plebiscito and the one of the lanes in the ancient centre. You start from the Neptune Fountain, pass the Maschio Angioino, the San Carlo and the Galleria, walk up Via Toledo and into the Decumani as far as San Gregorio Armeno. Then you go down beneath San Lorenzo Maggiore, where the Roman streets survive, ticket included. If you like, you finish with lunch.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Municipio, at the Neptune Fountain, with the time confirmed via the booking panel. The guide introduces the history of the city and you walk towards Castel Nuovo, the Teatro di San Carlo, the Galleria Umberto I, Piazza Trieste e Trento and Piazza del Plebiscito, the grand stretch of royal Naples.

From there you take Via Toledo into the old town: Via San Gregorio Armeno with its nativity-scene workshops, and Via dei Tribunali. Beneath the Basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore, the guided visit to the Roman remains lasts about three quarters of an hour, entry included. The three-hour tour ends between Piazza Bellini and Piazza del Gesù Nuovo.

If you choose the longer option, you stop for an hour for lunch: caprese, spaghetti with tomato sauce or carbonara, tiramisù, a glass of house wine and a bottle of water. In that case the tour ends after the meal. Groups can reach forty people, with headsets when needed to hear the guide clearly.
18971P22.perChi: For first-timers in Naples who want a clear picture of the city in one morning, from palaces to lanes, with a slice of the underground thrown in. There’s a fair amount of walking, so you need reasonable fitness. Less suited to anyone looking for a small group: it’s a large tour, with headsets.
18971P22.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and clothes for the weather, because the tour runs even in the rain. If you book lunch, flag allergies and intolerances straight away. Cruise passengers must give their ship and times when booking. The minimum is two participants from April to October, four in winter.

faq.q: How long is it and where do we meet?
faq.a: Three hours for the walk alone, four with lunch. The meeting point is Piazza Municipio, at the Neptune Fountain; the meeting time must be confirmed via the booking panel and differs from the listed start time.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The guided walking tour with a licensed guide, the ticket for the underground Roman ruins of San Lorenzo Maggiore and headsets when the group needs them. The meal is only included if you choose the lunch option. Tips and hotel transport are excluded.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English and Spanish. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. If the minimum number of participants isn’t reached, you’ll be offered an alternative or a refund.

18971P4.intro: A day on the Amalfi Coast that focuses on two towns instead of three: Amalfi, the old maritime republic, and Ravello, the village high up on the terraces. You travel in an air-conditioned vehicle with a tour leader on board who talks you through the coast, with photo stops and a limoncello tasting. Time in the towns is yours, with no compulsory guided visits, and if you like you can add a boat trip from Amalfi.
cosaSiFa: The driver picks you up at your hotel, where the service is available, or at the meeting point near the station, and you set off towards the Sorrento peninsula. The first stop is short, a quarter of an hour at a viewpoint for photos, before joining the coast road. Meanwhile the tour leader shares local stories and legends.

In Amalfi you have an hour and a half free: the Cathedral of Sant’Andrea, the squares, the harbour. The optional half-hour shared boat trip leaves from here, to see villas and cliffs from the sea. Then you climb to Ravello for an hour and a quarter: gardens, terraces and a calmer atmosphere. The drive back to Naples rounds off the day.
18971P4.perChi: For anyone who has already seen Positano or prefers the quieter side of the coast: Ravello is less crowded and has views no other town can match. Groups can reach thirty people, so it’s not an intimate tour. Not recommended for anyone with back problems, pregnant women or people with heart conditions: the road is all bends.
18971P4.consiglio: Choose the boat option when you book if you want to see Amalfi from the sea: half an hour is enough. In Ravello bring water and a hat, as you walk uphill and there’s little shade. Lunch isn’t included: you have more time in Amalfi, so that’s the place to eat. Confirm your pickup time beforehand, as it differs from the departure time.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: Eight hours in all. Pickup is door to door where possible, and the exact time is confirmed the day before. For last-minute bookings the only pickup point is near the station, in Piazza Garibaldi. The driver waits ten minutes for latecomers, then leaves.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: The tour leader speaks English, Italian, Spanish, French or Portuguese, depending on the date. The tour may run in two languages on the same day. It’s a shared group of up to thirty participants; in low season departure is confirmed with at least four people, in high season with two.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Return transport with air conditioning, a tour leader on board, photo stops, a limoncello tasting and water on request. The boat trip is only included if you choose that option. Lunch and tips are excluded. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

18971P46.intro: Two and a half hours on a sailing boat, in a group of up to twelve, leaving from Molo Marinelli and following the Naples coastline to Posillipo. You pass Castel dell’Ovo and the Bourbon-era villas overlooking the sea, with Vesuvius, Capri and the Sorrento peninsula in the background, and stop for a swim when the weather allows. On board there’s a welcome drink and something to nibble as the sun goes down.
cosaSiFa: You board at Molo Marinelli in the late afternoon, cast off and head out with the city sliding past alongside. The first stretch runs past Castel dell’Ovo, then you continue towards Posillipo, where the hill drops sheer into the water and the Bourbon villas are easier to see from the sea than from the road, because from the road you can hardly see them at all.

At Posillipo, if the sea is calm and the season allows, the boat stops for a swim. The water here is cleaner than you’d expect from a city this size, and diving in with a view of Vesuvius is usually the part that stays with you. If you’d rather not get wet, stay on board with a glass in hand.

On the way back comes the sunset: the welcome drink, a spritz, with some crunchy nibbles, and the bay changing colour with Capri and the Sorrento coast ahead. You get back to the jetty as darkness is almost falling, in time for dinner, with the salt still on your skin.
18971P46.perChi: For couples, groups of friends and anyone who wants to see Naples from the sea without the chaos of the ferries: twelve people at most, slow pace. Also fine if you’ve never set foot on a sailing boat. If you get seasick, think it over, and if you’re travelling with young children, bear in mind it’s two and a half hours on board without going ashore.
18971P46.consiglio: Bring a swimsuit and towel, ideally with the swimsuit already on, so no time is lost at Posillipo. You’ll also want a sweatshirt: out on the water at sunset the air changes, even in summer. The exact boarding point and time, which follows the sunset, come with your confirmation: be there a few minutes early. With only twelve places, book ahead.

faq.q: Where does the boat leave from and how long is it?
faq.a: It leaves from Molo Marinelli, in central Naples, and you’re at sea for about two and a half hours, with the timing following the sunset. Groups are up to twelve people. Italian, English, Spanish and French are spoken on board.

faq.q: Can we swim?
faq.a: Yes, there’s a swim stop in the waters off Posillipo, if sea conditions allow. Bring a swimsuit and towel. If you’d rather not get wet, stay on board: the boat is still and the view of Vesuvius is the same.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Small-group sailing, a welcome drink (a spritz) and some crunchy nibbles are included. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund.

18971P68.intro: A full day combining the three things everyone passing through Naples always asks for: the Amalfi Coast seen from above, Sorrento and Pompeii. You travel in an air-conditioned coach with commentary on board, stop to photograph the bay, taste limoncello where it’s made, get two free hours in Sorrento and finish with a guided visit to the ruins, ticket included. Designed for anyone short on time, cruise passengers included.
cosaSiFa: The coach collects participants at various points in Naples, including Molo Beverello, with the pickup time confirmed the day before based on where you’re staying. Along the Sorrento peninsula there are photo stops over the bay, then a twenty-minute stop at a limoncello workshop to taste the liqueur and other lemon products.

You continue to the panoramic terrace over Positano, a quarter of an hour to look down on the vertical village and take photos. Then Sorrento, with two free hours: the shopping street, the cloister of San Francesco, a gelato or lunch, which is only included if chosen when booking.

The afternoon is for Pompeii. The guide takes the group into the ruins for an hour and a half to two hours: the Forum, one of the baths, some shops and a domus (a Roman house). The ticket is included and there’s no need to queue at the ticket office. Towards evening the coach takes everyone back to Naples, to the same points where they were picked up in the morning.
18971P68.perChi: For anyone with just one day who wants to take in the coast, Sorrento and Pompeii without organising trains and ferries, cruise passengers included. Not suitable for anyone with back or cardiovascular problems, pregnant women or anyone who has trouble walking: Pompeii requires good fitness. Babies travel on a lap.
18971P68.consiglio: In Sorrento the two hours fly by: decide beforehand whether you’d rather have lunch or explore. Bring comfortable shoes and water for the ruins, which are sun-baked in the afternoon. The tour runs rain or shine, and in low season it needs at least six participants to be confirmed.

faq.q: Where does it start and at what time?
faq.a: Pickup is at various points in Naples, including Molo Beverello, and straight from the ship for cruise passengers. The exact time differs from the tour’s start time: it’s confirmed via the booking panel based on where you’re staying.

faq.q: What’s included and what isn’t?
faq.a: Return transport from Naples, panoramic stops, commentary on board, a live guide at Pompeii and the entry ticket to the ruins. Lunch is only included if selected when booking. Tips and optional activities are at your own expense.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English and Spanish and may run bilingually. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. The day lasts about eight hours, travel included.

209424P1.intro: Capri seen first from the sea and then from land, on the same day. You start with an hour in a gozzo, the island's traditional wooden boat, past caves and coves all along the coast. Then a minibus climbs to Anacapri, where you get a couple of hours for the village, the chairlift up Monte Solaro or lunch. You finish in Capri town, with the Piazzetta, the lanes of designer boutiques and the Giardini di Augusto looking out over the Faraglioni rocks.
cosaSiFa: You meet in the morning at the port of Naples, at Molo Beverello, or mid-morning directly at Marina Grande if you're already on the island. First up is the boat: a full one-hour loop around Capri in a gozzo, with the caves, the coves and the Faraglioni seen from the water. It's the part that stays with you longest.

Once ashore, a minibus takes you up to Anacapri, the upper part of the island. You have about two hours here: the village is easy to explore on foot, and you can take the chairlift up Monte Solaro (extra cost) or stop for something to eat. Then it's down to Capri town: the Piazzetta, the boutique-lined lanes and the Giardini di Augusto, the terrace with the best view of the Faraglioni.
209424P1.perChi: For anyone who wants it all in one go: sea, Anacapri and Capri town, without piecing it together themselves. The guide speaks English, Spanish and Italian. It's wheelchair accessible and suitable for all fitness levels, and pushchairs are allowed. Groups are up to twenty people. If you get seasick, think carefully about the hour on the boat.
209424P1.consiglio: Bring sunglasses, sun cream and a hat: there's no shade on a gozzo for an hour. Wear walking shoes, as there are plenty of steps between Anacapri and Capri's lanes. If you book the option starting from Capri, you buy your own ferry ticket. Lunch isn't included: Anacapri, with its two hours, is the place to eat.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long does it last?
faq.a: At the port of Naples, Molo Beverello, at 8:30am; or at Marina Grande on the island at 10:30am if you choose the option from Capri. The day lasts between eight and nine hours, including the return.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The one-hour boat tour, the minibus on the island, the guide in English, Spanish and Italian, the visit to Anacapri and Capri, and entry to the Giardini di Augusto. It doesn't include lunch, the Monte Solaro chairlift or tips. The ferry isn't included in the option from Capri.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children and people with limited mobility? Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes: it's listed as wheelchair accessible and suitable for all fitness levels, with prams and pushchairs allowed. Infants travel on an adult's lap. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure.

23258P122.intro: Two hours in the Herculaneum ruins with an archaeologist, in a group of no more than fifteen, with ticket and earpieces included. Herculaneum is smaller than Pompeii but better preserved: the eruption of AD 79 covered it with a layer that kept the air out, so the charred wood of beams and furniture survived, along with mosaics and paintings whose colours are almost intact. It was a town of merchants and nobles, and it shows.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the ruins and go in with the ticket already bought by the operator. With the earpieces you can hear the archaeologist even when you drift a little away from the group. You start at the ancient shoreline: the remains of more than three hundred people who were waiting to escape by sea were found along the waterfront, and it's the hardest moment of the visit.

Then you climb up into the streets of the town. The planned stops are the Samnite House, the baths, the Temple of the Augustales, the forum, the House of Neptune and Amphitrite with its mosaic, the gymnasium and the House of the Wooden Partition. The archaeologist explains what you're looking at and what sets Herculaneum apart from Pompeii, starting with the charred wood and the colours of the paintings.

Two hours isn't enough to cover the whole site: the visit is a considered selection, with time for questions, which is the real advantage of a group of fifteen. The pace is relaxed and you stop for a good while in front of the best-preserved mosaics and frescoes.
23258P122.perChi: Ideal if you have half a day and want to really understand what you're looking at: the archaeologist makes all the difference compared with going on your own. The small group also helps with teenagers. You walk for two hours outdoors on ancient streets, so you need proper shoes. If you want to see the whole site at leisure, add some time after the tour.
23258P122.consiglio: You reach Herculaneum from Naples on the Circumvesuviana, getting off at Ercolano Scavi, and the two-hour tour leaves the afternoon free to add Vesuvius, just a few kilometres away. In summer pick the morning slot: there's little shade inside. Hat, water and closed shoes.

faq.q: Is the entry ticket included?
faq.a: Yes. The price includes entry to the Herculaneum ruins, the two-hour guided visit with an archaeologist, and earpieces so you can follow the explanation even from a distance. The group is limited to fifteen people.

faq.q: What languages is the tour in?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English, German, Spanish and French. You choose the language when you book and the group is formed accordingly, always with an archaeologist as guide.

faq.q: How long does it last and how do I cancel?
faq.a: About two hours, all inside the ruins, starting from the site entrance. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the tour's start time.

276598P12.intro: Forty-five minutes in the Sansevero Chapel with a licensed guide, ticket included. The star is the Veiled Christ, the marble statue whose veil looks like fabric; around it are the other Baroque statues commissioned by Raimondo di Sangro, the prince who had the whole place built, and in the crypt the two Anatomical Machines, skeletons with their circulatory systems reconstructed. Without an explanation you see a chapel; with the guide you understand what lies behind it.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, with the guide at the chapel entrance, a few steps from the square. You go in with the ticket already bought, and the guide starts with the story of Prince Raimondo di Sangro, who commissioned the chapel, and the esoteric symbols hidden among the Baroque sculptures.

Then you stop in front of the Veiled Christ: the guide explains how it was carved and tells the legends that grew up around the marble veil. You go round the other sculptures and finally head down into the crypt, home to the Anatomical Machines. Forty-five minutes in all, with a group of no more than twenty.
276598P12.perChi: Good if you're short on time and want the most famous thing in the old town with a proper explanation, without worrying about tickets. Fine for families with children who can manage 45 minutes of listening. If you'd rather look in silence, without a group, you can buy a standard ticket; here the value is the guide.
276598P12.consiglio: After the chapel you're in the heart of Spaccanapoli: San Domenico Maggiore, the Nile statue and Via San Gregorio Armeno are a few minutes' walk away. Book ahead, especially at weekends and on Italian bank holidays, because the chapel is small and time slots sell out fast.

faq.q: Is the ticket included?
faq.a: Yes, the entry ticket to the Sansevero Chapel is included, along with the visit with a licensed guide. The visit also includes going down into the crypt with the Anatomical Machines, as well as the Veiled Christ and the other sculptures.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: About 45 minutes. The meeting point is Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, with the guide waiting at the chapel entrance. Groups are no more than twenty people.

faq.q: What languages is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is in Italian, English or French, chosen when you book. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start of the visit.

297875P1.intro: Two hours in a pizzeria on Via San Carlo, opposite the opera house, with an English-speaking pizzaiolo who gets your hands in the dough. It's not a demonstration: you make the dough yourself, starting from the flour, then slice the mozzarella and prepare the tomato. You eat what you've made, with bruschetta first and tiramisù after, drink included. Groups of up to fifteen.
cosaSiFa: The first part is theory and practice on the dough: the pizzaiolo explains the ingredients and the technique, then everyone kneads their own dough ball following his lead. Meanwhile the bruschetta arrives. Then on to the toppings: you slice the mozzarella and make the tomato sauce with fresh ingredients supplied by the pizzeria.

Next you stretch your pizza, it goes in the oven and you eat it in the pizzeria with a drink. The tiramisù, which shares top billing with the pizza, rounds off the meal. Two hours in all, in English. At the end you walk out onto Via San Carlo, with the theatre in front of you and Piazza del Plebiscito just round the corner.
297875P1.perChi: Good if you speak English and want to learn dough from a real pizzaiolo, in a working pizzeria rather than a teaching kitchen. Suits couples, friends and families; two hours is manageable with children too. If you can't follow English, you'll miss the explanations. The location, opposite the San Carlo, makes it easy to fit into a day in the centre.
297875P1.consiglio: Don't have lunch beforehand: bruschetta, pizza and tiramisù are plenty. The class is opposite Teatro San Carlo and a step from Galleria Umberto I and Piazza del Plebiscito: arrive a little early and have a wander. Wear clothes that can take some flour, and come with clean hands.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: A theory and hands-on class with an English-speaking pizzaiolo, fresh ingredients and equipment, bruschetta, the pizza you've made, tiramisù and a drink. You eat everything in the pizzeria, so it counts as a full meal.

faq.q: How long does it last and where is it held?
faq.a: About two hours, in a pizzeria on Via San Carlo in central Naples, opposite the theatre. Groups are no more than fifteen people. The exact address comes with your booking confirmation.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The class is in English, with an English-speaking pizzaiolo. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before the class starts.

299918P1.intro: Two hours on a farm in Massa Lubrense, at the tip of the Sorrento peninsula, to see where the Sorrento lemon comes from before it ends up in a bottle. You see the seedbed, the field of mother plants and a graft made right in front of you, walk under the traditional pergola and climb to a viewpoint looking out to Ischia, Procida and the Bay of Naples. Along the way you taste what the farm produces: lemonade, limoncello, cream of limoncello, orange and cinnamon liqueur, jams and olive oil. The meeting point is the bus stop in the main square of Massa Lubrense, with departures at 10am and 5pm.
cosaSiFa: The guide meets you at the EAV and SITA bus stop in the village square and walks you to the farm. You start sitting down, with a glass of lemonade and lemon slices with sugar, which is how they're eaten round here, peel and all. Then into the seedbed: this is where bitter orange seeds are planted, because the Sorrento lemon doesn't grow on its own roots but on those of a sturdier plant.

From the seedbed you move on to the field of mother plants, the mature trees from which the cutting for the graft is taken. The next stop is the viewpoint: from there you can see Ischia, Procida, the whole Bay of Naples and the centre of Massa Lubrense. You stop for photos and the first round of tastings, limoncello, cream of limoncello and orange and cinnamon liqueur, while the guide tells how the lemon reached this coast.

After the break comes the part almost nobody has ever seen: grafting. The guide shows how the rootstock is cut, how the cutting is inserted and how it's tied, then shows you young plants already grafted, at various stages of growth. It's the moment you understand why a lemon grove takes years before it bears fruit.

The way back runs under the Sorrento pergola, the structure of chestnut poles and netting that shields the lemons from wind and cold and turns these plots into green corridors. You finish back at the start with lemon and ginger jam and orange and cinnamon jam, a drizzle of olive oil and a few minutes to sit down before heading back to the square.
299918P1.perChi: For anyone on holiday in Sorrento or on the peninsula who wants a slow half-day away from the crowded main street, and for families: there's little walking, on easy ground, pushchairs can get through and children from two up have their own rate. It also works if you know nothing about farming, because the guide starts from the basics. Less suited to anyone after a proper walk or trail scenery: you stay on the farm, and the point is understanding how a lemon grove works, not clocking up miles.
299918P1.consiglio: Pick the 5pm slot between May and September: it's cooler under the pergola and from the viewpoint the bay catches the late-afternoon light. If you're coming from Naples, allow more than an hour and a half between the Circumvesuviana train to Sorrento and the SITA bus to Massa Lubrense, so catch an early train. If you're driving, stick to one small glass: the tastings are generous. Bring an empty bag, because you can buy the jams and liqueurs at the farm.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: About two hours. You meet at the EAV and SITA bus stop in the main square of Massa Lubrense, and that's where you finish. There are two departures a day, at 10am and 5pm, every day of the week. Pick-up from some hotels in the area can be requested when you book.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The guided farm visit and all the tastings: lemonade and lemon slices with sugar on arrival, limoncello, cream of limoncello and orange and cinnamon liqueur at the viewpoint, citrus jams and olive oil at the end. Transport to Massa Lubrense isn't included, except pick-up where available. Prices start at €45 per person.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children?
faq.a: Yes. The route is easy, you can do it with a pushchair and there's a children's rate for ages two to fourteen. Bookings must be made by an adult. The liqueurs are for grown-ups, of course, but the lemonade, sugared lemons and jams are for everyone.

faq.q: What language is the tour in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks Italian and English. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before departure with a full refund, and if the weather rules out the visit it's cancelled, with the option to change date or get a refund. You can book up to ten people at a time.

30791P767.intro: Half a day on foot with a Neapolitan acting as your host, just for your group of up to eight. There's no fixed route: after booking you fill in a short form with your interests and the host gets in touch to build the itinerary, whether that's the Rione Sanità, the markets, hidden courtyards or spots with a view of the bay. You start from your hotel and go on for two to six hours.
cosaSiFa: Before you even set off: after booking you get an online form where you note what interests you, what you've already seen and what you don't want to miss. The local host writes to you personally and suggests a made-to-measure tour: history, food, neighbourhoods or a mix of everything.

On the day, the host picks you up at your hotel and you walk. Depending on what you've chosen, you might go among the stalls of a street market, into the lanes of the Rione Sanità, into the courtyards of old palazzi, to family-run bars or up to one of the spots overlooking the bay.

There's no group of strangers: it's you and the host, so you set the pace, with breaks when you need them. How long it lasts depends on the option booked, from two to six hours, and the content changes from group to group.
30791P767.perChi: For anyone who doesn't want to follow a guide's umbrella and would rather have a tour made for them: families with children of different ages, groups of up to eight friends, people on their second trip to Naples who've already seen the main sights. Makes less sense if you have three hours in total and just want the list of monuments: that's what the classic tours are for.
30791P767.consiglio: Fill in the form carefully, it's what shapes the day: say whether you enjoy walking, whether you have children, whether you've already done the old town. Comfortable shoes either way. If you go for the longer version, ask to take in the Sanità or Posillipo, which are harder to navigate on foot on your own.

faq.q: How does the personalisation work?
faq.a: After booking you receive an online form to note your interests and preferences. The host contacts you personally and builds a made-to-measure itinerary: history, food, neighbourhoods or lesser-known places, based on what you've written.

faq.q: How long does it last and for how many people?
faq.a: From two to six hours, depending on the option chosen. It's a private tour for your group, up to eight people, starting from your hotel.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: English and Italian. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

308572P2.intro: Two hours inside the Herculaneum ruins with a guide licensed by the Campania Region and a group of no more than fifteen. Herculaneum was buried by the same eruption of AD 79 that covered Pompeii, but here pyroclastic flows buried it under twenty metres of scorching material and preserved it better: it's smaller, it was wealthier, and the original decoration can still be seen in the houses. Explanations in Italian, English or German. The entry ticket is bought separately.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the entrance to the Herculaneum ruins. The guide sets out the difference from Pompeii straight away: same eruption, different effects. Here it was pyroclastic flows, a mass of scorching ash, that swept into the houses, sealed them and hid them twenty metres below the level of the modern town, which now towers above them. They've stayed that way for almost two thousand years.

You then walk through the streets and homes of what was a residential town for wealthy families: you go into the houses to see the original decoration, the floors and details that were lost at Pompeii. The guide chooses the stops based on the group and the areas open that day, and explains why two cities struck by the same disaster have come down to us so differently. Two hours in all, with no more than fifteen people, so you hear everything without headsets.
308572P2.perChi: For anyone who's already seen Pompeii or prefers a more compact site, one you can properly understand in two hours rather than half a day of walking: couples, families with older children, ancient history lovers. The small group helps if you like to ask questions. Less suited to anyone after the scale and crowds of Pompeii, or who doesn't want to pay for the ticket separately.
308572P2.consiglio: Buy your entry ticket before the meeting time, because it isn't included. Hat, water and closed shoes: you're outdoors and walking over stones. Herculaneum is reached from Naples on the Circumvesuviana and is on the way to Vesuvius: ruins in the morning and crater in the afternoon, or the other way round, makes a full but doable day.

faq.q: Is the entry ticket included?
faq.a: No. The price covers the Region-licensed guide for two hours in a group of no more than fifteen; entry to the ruins is bought separately and must be done before the meeting time, so the group can go in on schedule. Explanations are in Italian, English or German.

faq.q: How long does it last and how many people are there?
faq.a: The visit lasts about two hours and the group is limited to fifteen. It's a format designed for understanding the site at an easy pace, going into the houses and asking questions without having to chase after a big tour group. You meet at the Herculaneum ruins.

faq.q: Herculaneum or Pompeii?
faq.a: They're different: Pompeii is huge and needs half a day; Herculaneum is smaller, was wealthier and is better preserved, with the house decoration still easy to read. If you're short on time or have already been to Pompeii, Herculaneum in two hours gives you more. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

353209P1.intro: Three hours by boat along the Posillipo coast with a marine biologist and a licensed guide, in a group of no more than ten. You leave from the pier on Via Caracciolo, cruise past caves carved out by the Romans, snorkel with the gear provided (wetsuit included in the colder months) and land on a little beach known almost only to Neapolitans. Beer and taralli (crunchy Neapolitan savoury biscuits) on board, with a deck shower, sun canopy and fridge.
cosaSiFa: You board at the Via Caracciolo pier and, as the boat pulls away from the seafront, the guide tells the story of the city seen from the sea while the biologist explains what lives in these waters. The boat is set up for comfort: deck shower, music, a canopy for shade, fridge and cushions.

Once below the Posillipo hill you pass the Roman-era caves cut into the rock and make the first stop for swimming and snorkelling. Mask and snorkel are provided, plus a wetsuit in the colder months. If you can't swim, you can still get in the water and stay close to the boat.

The next stop is Villa Lauro, where you land on a small, tucked-away beach with a view of the bay. Throughout the trip you're offered drinks and nibbles, beer and taralli. You're back at the starting pier after about three hours.
353209P1.perChi: For anyone who wants to see Naples from the water without the crowds of the big boats: couples, friends, families with children over two. Non-swimmers can still come and get in the water beside the boat. If you get seasick, bring your own medication. Children under two aren't allowed.
353209P1.consiglio: Swimsuit on already, towel, hat and sun cream, and a bag that can get wet. Calm-sea days are best for snorkelling: if the weather turns, the trip can be cancelled up to half an hour before. Before or after, the seafront and Castel dell'Ovo are a short walk from the pier.

faq.q: What's included in the boat trip?
faq.a: The licensed guide, the marine biologist, snorkelling gear with a wetsuit in the colder months, and drinks and nibbles on board, beer and taralli. The boat has a deck shower, canopy, fridge, cushions and music. The group is no more than ten people.

faq.q: Do I need to be able to swim?
faq.a: No. Non-swimmers can get in the water and stay close to the boat. Children under two can't take part. If you get seasick, bring your own medication, as none is provided on board.

faq.q: What language is it in, and how does cancellation work?
faq.a: English, Spanish and Italian. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before. In bad weather the trip can be cancelled up to half an hour before departure. The starting point is the Via Caracciolo pier, on the seafront.

39613P103.intro: Two and a half hours between the Naples above ground and the Naples below. You start in Piazza Bellini, go down into the tunnels and chambers beneath San Lorenzo, where the remains of the Roman city lie, with the market, the public buildings and traces of the forum, then climb back up to walk along Spaccanapoli to San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene workshops. Entry to Neapolis Sotterrata and guide included, groups of up to fifteen.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Bellini. From there the guide leads the group through the streets of the centre, stopping along the way to explain what you're seeing, and takes everyone to the entrance of the excavations beneath San Lorenzo Maggiore, where the underground part begins.

Below ground you walk through passages, tunnels and excavated rooms: the level of the Roman city, with the market square, the public buildings and what's left of the forum. The guide explains how this layer stayed intact beneath a city that kept growing on top of it, century after century.

You come back up into daylight and carry on along Spaccanapoli, the dead-straight street that cuts through the old town, with the everyday life of its shops and lanes. You finish in San Gregorio Armeno, among the stalls of artisans who make nativity scenes all year round.
39613P103.perChi: For first-timers in Naples who want the old town and what lies beneath it in one go. Good for couples, friends and families with older children; groups are no more than fifteen. You walk for two and a half hours, with stairs down and back up: bear that in mind if you have mobility issues.
39613P103.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and a light sweatshirt: underground the temperature drops, even in summer. Mornings are best, when Spaccanapoli is still bearable. You finish in San Gregorio Armeno: from there the Duomo and the Sansevero Chapel are five minutes' walk away, handy for filling the afternoon.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: The guide and entry to Neapolis Sotterrata, the archaeological site beneath San Lorenzo. The tour lasts two and a half hours, in groups of up to fifteen.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: English and Italian, chosen when you book.

faq.q: Where do we meet, and can I cancel?
faq.a: In Piazza Bellini, in the old town. The route ends in San Gregorio Armeno. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

39613P228.intro: The royal palace Charles of Bourbon commissioned in 1750 to rival Europe's great courts: 1,200 rooms, designed by Luigi Vanvitelli, with a park that seems to go on forever. With a group of no more than sixteen you skip the queue, climb the Grand Staircase and walk through the Royal Apartments, then the shuttle takes you to the far end of the park, past fountains and the waterfall, to the English Garden. Three hours, and at the end you're free to stay on in the grounds.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Carlo di Borbone, at the palace's main entrance, ten minutes before your time. With priority tickets you go straight in, and the first hour and a half is spent in the palace: the Grand Staircase, the chapel, the Royal Apartments with frescoes, gilding and Baroque furniture, and the little court theatre, a miniature echo of the San Carlo. Groups over seven use headsets.

The second part is in the park. You board the shuttle bus included in the price and ride up to the top of the gardens, with fountains and sculptures inspired by classical mythology and the waterfall. From there the guide takes you into the English Garden, full of exotic plants and flowers, where the visit ends.

The tour finishes there, in the middle of the English Garden: if you like, you can stay on and explore the gardens on your own, with no need to keep to the group's schedule, perhaps walking back down the avenues and pools towards the palace. Getting back to Caserta or Naples is up to you, as is getting there.
39613P228.perChi: For anyone who wants to see the palace without losing an hour in the queue or wearing themselves out on three kilometres of avenues: the shuttle sorts that. Suitable for all fitness levels, but it isn't wheelchair accessible and isn't recommended for anyone with back problems. Guide dogs are allowed.
39613P228.consiglio: Comfortable shoes, because between the rooms and the gardens you still walk a fair bit. Getting to the meeting point isn't covered by the tour: from Naples the train to Caserta is your best bet, as the station is a short walk from the palace. After the visit, if you have time, stay in the gardens until closing.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: Three hours: an hour and a half in the palace and an hour and a half in the park. Meet in Piazza Carlo di Borbone, in front of the palace's main entrance, at least ten minutes before the start, with your voucher on your phone or printed.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The three-hour guided visit, skip-the-line tickets for the palace, the English Garden ticket, the shuttle to get there and headsets for groups over seven. Tips and transport to the meeting point aren't included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian and English, depending on the date. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. Groups are no more than sixteen people.

420535P5.intro: An hour and a half by boat along the Naples coast, from the Borgo Marinari to the waters off Posillipo, with no more than nine people on board. You pass beneath Castel dell'Ovo and in front of Palazzo Donn'Anna, the unfinished palace that rises straight out of the sea, while the skipper tells stories of the city and its life on the water. When conditions allow, you stop for a swim: soft drinks and snorkelling masks are included. It's the quickest way to see Naples the way the fishermen saw it.
cosaSiFa: You leave from the Borgo Marinari, the little harbour at the foot of Castel dell'Ovo. As soon as you're out of the harbour the castle is right there, seen from the side you can't see from land, and the boat follows the seafront towards Posillipo. The group is small, no more than nine people, so there's no rush and you can chat with the skipper without jostling for space.

You carry on to Palazzo Donn'Anna, which from the sea you can see in full, its façade dropping straight into the water. In the most sheltered stretch, off Posillipo, the boat stops for swimming and snorkelling: the masks are on board, along with the soft drinks. Throughout the trip the skipper talks about the history of the coast and Neapolitan seafaring culture, with stories about the palazzi and the caves you can only see from here. You're back at the Borgo Marinari after about an hour and a half, with time to dry off before you step ashore.
420535P5.perChi: Designed for couples, families and groups of friends who want a break from the heat and the lanes without going all the way to Capri. Also good if you're short on time, because ninety minutes later you're back on dry land on the seafront. Less suited to anyone who gets seasick or doesn't want to get wet: the swim is the part everyone looks forward to.
420535P5.consiglio: Swimsuit on already, towel and sun cream, because you'll be swimming and there's little shade on the boat. The hour before sunset gives the best light on Vesuvius. Before or after, walk round Castel dell'Ovo and grab something on Via Partenope. On summer weekends, book a few days ahead.

faq.q: How many people are on board?
faq.a: No more than nine. It's a small boat, designed precisely to keep away from the crowded ones: you can hear the skipper without a microphone, switch sides for photos with no trouble, and the swimming stop is more relaxed. Explanations are in Italian or English.

faq.q: What's included and what should I bring?
faq.a: Soft drinks and snorkelling masks are included. Bring a swimsuit, towel, sun cream and a light sweatshirt for the ride back if you go out towards evening. The trip lasts about an hour and a half, starting and finishing at the Borgo Marinari, below Castel dell'Ovo.

faq.q: Can I cancel if the weather is bad?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund. If the sea is too rough to go out, the operator will offer you another time or a refund: either way, it's best not to leave the decision to the last minute.

51159P8.intro: Three hours on foot in the old town, in a group of no more than twelve, eating what Neapolitans actually eat on the street. This isn’t a parade of tiny nibbles: there are at least four stops, a drink is included, and by the end you’ve had a proper meal. Your guide is a local who explains every dish, where it comes from and why it’s eaten the way it is. The meeting point is Piazza Dante.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Dante and head straight into the lanes of the old town. The route mixes walking and stops: each one is a place chosen for a specific dish, from the great classics of Neapolitan street food to everyday things tourists usually don’t know about. Between bites you talk about history and the habits of the neighbourhood.

There are at least four stops, and one drink is included. The group is small, twelve people at most, so you don’t wait long at the counter and you can ask questions. The tour is always run in English and Italian together; other languages can be requested when booking, but aren’t guaranteed.

After about three hours you finish with a full stomach and a mental map of the old town that no printed guide gives you: the places where you ate stay with you, and you can find them again on your own over the next few days, perhaps at lunchtime, when the queue is made of Neapolitans.
51159P8.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants to get Neapolitan food in one afternoon, and for solo travellers: in a group of twelve you bond quickly. Good for couples and friends. If you struggle with three hours of walking on old paving stones or have food intolerances to manage, think it through and flag it in advance. Not designed for anyone who has already had lunch.
51159P8.consiglio: Go on an empty stomach and in comfortable shoes: the old town’s lanes are stone and up-and-down. Piazza Dante sits where Via Toledo meets the decumani, the old town’s ancient main streets, so Spaccanapoli and Via dei Tribunali pair well before or after. With twelve places per tour, book a few days ahead, especially at weekends.

faq.q: How many stops are there and what’s included?
faq.a: There are at least four stops, each with a different taste of Neapolitan street food, plus one drink. Altogether it adds up to a full meal, not a snack. The guide is included and the group never goes over twelve people. The tour lasts about three hours.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: Always in English and Italian, bilingually, so Neapolitans and visitors can share the same group. Other languages can be requested when booking, with no guarantee. The starting point is Piazza Dante, in the old town.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. If you have allergies or don’t eat certain foods, say so when you book, before the tour is organised.

51159P9.intro: Three hours on foot in the old town with a guide who eats for a living, in a group of no more than 12. Starting from Piazza Dante you make at least four stops: pizza first, then the street food Neapolitans eat every day, from the classics to the ones tourists rarely hear about. At each stop the guide explains the dish and the story behind it. One drink is included. The tour is in English and Italian at the same time.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Dante and head straight into the ancient centre. The first part is all about pizza, the reason most people come to Naples, eaten where the locals eat it. Then you carry on through the lanes with at least three more street food stops.

The stops are chosen to show how people really eat in the city: the classics everyone knows, and the everyday things tourists tend to skip. The guide explains each dish, tells the stories of the places and adds the kind of tips you’d give a friend about what to do over the next few days.

The group is small, 12 people at most, so you can actually talk to the guide. Commentary is always in English and Italian together; other languages need to be requested in advance. Three hours of slow walking in all, with one drink included. It’s more a long meal than a walk.
51159P9.perChi: For people who love eating and want to go beyond the margherita, with time to stop and ask. Works for couples, friends and solo travellers, because the groups are small. Three hours is a lot if you only have one day in Naples; if you have two, this is a good way to start the first.
51159P9.consiglio: Arrive hungry, seriously. Piazza Dante has its own metro stop, easy from anywhere in the city. After the tour you’re a short walk from Via Toledo and the Quartieri Spagnoli. Comfortable shoes and, in the hot months, the coolest slot of the day. There are twelve places: book a few days ahead.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it start?
faq.a: About three hours, on foot, starting from Piazza Dante, on the edge of the old town. The pace is slow, with at least four stops to eat; it isn’t a long walk, but you’re on your feet quite a bit.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The tastings at the stops, at least four, and one drink, plus the guide. Pizza is the first stop, then comes the rest of Neapolitan street food. The tastings are meant to replace a meal; anything extra you order at the counter is on you.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour always runs in English and Italian at the same time; other languages can be requested when booking. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund.

5512754P7.intro: At Baia, in the Campi Flegrei (the Phlegraean Fields west of Naples), the Roman villas that once stood on the shore ended up underwater because of bradyseism, the slow sinking of the volcanic ground. Today they lie about four metres down and you can see them clearly from the surface: all you need is a mask. You head out by boat from Baia harbour in a group of no more than eight, with guide and gear included, and in two and a half hours you swim over the floors, walls and streets of a Roman town now lived in by fish.
cosaSiFa: You meet at Baia harbour and board the boat with the guide, who explains on the way what happened here: the Roman resort town of luxury, the volcanic activity of the Campi Flegrei, and the bradyseism that over the centuries pulled the coast below sea level. You’re given a mask and gear and arrive above the underwater park.

Then you get in and snorkel over the remains of the villas: at no more than four metres deep, you can make out the structures from the surface without diving down. The guide points out what you’re looking at and the marine life that has settled around it. The group is eight people at most, so nobody gets left behind in the water and there’s time to ask questions. Then it’s back on board and back to the harbour: about two and a half hours in all, with commentary in Italian or English.
5512754P7.perChi: For anyone who can swim and wants to see something with no equal around Naples, as a couple, with friends or with teenagers who are comfortable in the water. The group is eight at most, so the guide keeps an eye on everyone. Less suited to anyone uneasy in open water or wanting to stay on board: swimming is the whole point here.
5512754P7.consiglio: Go on a calm, sunny day, when the water is clearest and the ruins are easiest to see. Swimsuit on underneath, a towel, sun cream and a spare towel. While you’re in Baia, add the Castello Aragonese and its archaeological museum of the Campi Flegrei. Book a few days ahead, there are only eight places.

faq.q: Do I need snorkelling or diving experience?
faq.a: You just need to be able to swim and feel comfortable with a mask and snorkel: the remains are no more than four metres down and visible from the surface, with no diving involved. Gear is included and the guide stays with the group, which is eight people at most.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it leave from?
faq.a: About two and a half hours, including the boat ride, the explanations and time in the water. You leave from Baia harbour, in the Campi Flegrei, and return to the same spot. Commentary is in Italian or English.

faq.q: What happens if the sea is rough?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before with a full refund. If sea conditions don’t allow the trip or make the water cloudy, you’re usually offered another day: it’s worth booking early in your stay to leave some margin.

5921P19.intro: Half a day on Vesuvius devoted to wine. You leave Naples in the late morning with a pick-up near where you’re staying, head up into the vineyards on the slopes of the volcano and walk between the rows with a guide who explains what grows in lava soil. Then you sit down: a full Mediterranean lunch with Falanghina, Lacryma Christi, Aglianico and other local wines. Four hours in all, transport included, groups of up to 15.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the pick-up point nearest your accommodation, at around eleven. From there the organised transport takes you up to the slopes of Vesuvius, where the vineyards are. With the guide you stroll between the rows: it isn’t a demanding walk, you go slowly, look at the vines, take in the smells and hear how volcanic soil changes the wine.

The second part is at the table. Lunch is a full Mediterranean meal, served with local wines: Falanghina, Lacryma Christi, Aglianico and other typical labels, paired with the courses. You stay seated for a good while, the way people do in the countryside. At the end the same transport brings you back to Naples. About four hours in total.
The tour runs with a minimum of two people and a maximum of 15, so the table stays intimate. The guide speaks Italian or English.
5921P19.perChi: For wine lovers who want to understand what Vesuvius puts in the glass, and for anyone after a slow day after several days in the old town. Good for couples and friends. If you only have one day in Naples, think about whether to give four hours to this; if you don’t drink you’ll still get a good lunch, but you’re mostly paying for the tasting.
5921P19.consiglio: Light breakfast: lunch is generous and there’s more than one wine. Comfortable closed shoes for the vineyards, a hat in summer. If you like, the next day you can go up to the Vesuvius crater or visit the ruins of Herculaneum, which are on the same side of the mountain. Book early: the tour runs with two people, but there are only fifteen places.

faq.q: How does the pick-up work and how long does it last?
faq.a: The tour lasts about 4 hours. You meet at the pick-up point nearest your accommodation, in the late morning, from those set by the organisers; the return to Naples is included. Departure is guaranteed with just two participants.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: Transport to and from Naples, the guided walk through the vineyards, the tasting and a full Mediterranean lunch with Falanghina, Lacryma Christi, Aglianico and other typical Vesuvius wines.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks Italian and English. The group is 15 people at most. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund; after that there’s no refund.

71024P23.intro: Under the arcades of the Galleria Principe di Napoli there’s a small room where, for an hour, the Neapolitan repertoire is sung and danced with no microphones: ’O sole mio, Torna a Surriento, Anema e core and the tarantella. The group is small, ten people at most, and you sit a few metres from the musicians. It isn’t a theatre concert but something homely, with a welcome drink and the whole room singing together at the end.
cosaSiFa: You come in, pick up your welcome drink and take a seat. With ten people at most there are no bad seats: everyone can see the hands on the instruments and hear the singers breathe. There are no amplifiers or microphones, and you notice straight away, because the sound is the real sound of voices and strings.

The programme runs through the Neapolitan songs the whole world knows, from Torna a Surriento to Anema e core, with a few words on what the lyrics mean, since Neapolitan isn’t always clear to outsiders. Then comes the tarantella, danced as well as played. Just under an hour in all, without long breaks, with the show presented in Italian.

The finale is ’O sole mio, and they don’t sing it alone: the whole room joins in, because it’s the one song everyone knows by heart, Neapolitans and visitors alike. Then you’re back in the Galleria, a short walk from the Archaeological Museum and the old town, with the rest of the evening free.
71024P23.perChi: For anyone who wants to hear Neapolitan song up close rather than from the stalls: couples, solo travellers, people travelling with their parents. The group of ten also suits anyone who doesn’t like crowded venues. If you’re after a big show with sets and an orchestra, this isn’t it; here it’s all about voice, instruments and closeness.
71024P23.consiglio: With only ten seats it’s worth booking a few days ahead, especially at weekends. The Galleria Principe is next to the Archaeological Museum: if you arrive early you can look around there first, or have an aperitivo in Piazza Bellini, five minutes’ walk away. It’s just one hour, so it pairs nicely with dinner afterwards.

faq.q: How many people take part and what language is it in?
faq.a: The group is small, ten people at most, and the show is presented in Italian. The songs, of course, are in Neapolitan, but everyone sings along to the ’O sole mio finale, wherever they’re from. The concert lasts about an hour.

faq.q: What does the ticket include?
faq.a: Entry to the concert of about an hour and a welcome drink. The meeting point is in the Galleria Principe di Napoli, in Piazza Museo, next to the National Archaeological Museum. Nothing else is included: you arrive, have a drink and sit a few steps from the musicians.

faq.q: How does cancellation work?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. As there are only ten seats per show, if you know you can’t make it, cancel in good time so someone else can take your place.

71024P92.intro: Two hours on foot along the decumani, the straight streets laid out by the Greeks and kept by the Romans, with Spaccanapoli in the middle. You start from Piazza Dante and go past churches, workshops and the San Gregorio Armeno market, where nativity figures sit alongside pagan lucky charms. The group is twenty people at most, the guide speaks four languages, and along the way there’s a tasting, sweet or savoury.
cosaSiFa: From Piazza Dante you enter the Greco-Roman grid: straight streets, narrow lanes and a church every few metres. The guide explains why Naples has the Greek street plan, Roman remains, the Middle Ages and the Baroque all at once, and helps you spot them one by one on the façades, moving from one era to the next in a few steps.

Spaccanapoli is the lower decumanus, the dead-straight slit that cuts through the old town from end to end. Along the way you come to San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity scenes, with the artisans’ workshops open and the mix of Christian and pagan symbols that’s perfectly normal here. You stop, go in and watch them work.

At some point comes the included tasting, sweet or savoury, to show how Neapolitan culture also travels through food. In the lanes you may well come across street musicians and dancers, part of the show without being on the programme. After two hours you’re free again, right in the heart of the old town.
71024P92.perChi: For first-timers in Naples who want a key to reading the old town before exploring it alone. Good for couples, families and solo travellers; with twenty people at most you’re in a group without getting lost. Two hours on paving stones and lanes: comfortable shoes are a must, pushchairs are hard work.
71024P92.consiglio: Do it on your first day: afterwards you’ll explore the old town on your own with different eyes. Piazza Dante has a metro stop, handy for arriving on time. At the end you’re a short walk from the Cristo Velato (Veiled Christ), the Duomo and Napoli Sotterranea, which are booked separately. The lanes are more pleasant in the morning than in the afternoon.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long does it last?
faq.a: The meeting point is Piazza Dante, at the entrance to the old town, and the tour lasts two hours, all on foot along the decumani and Spaccanapoli as far as San Gregorio Armeno. The group is twenty people at most. Available times show up when you select a date.

faq.q: Which languages is it available in?
faq.a: Italian, English, Spanish and French. You choose the language when booking. The route crosses the Greek and Roman city, the medieval one and the Baroque one, and the guide helps you recognise them on the façades and in the churches.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: The guide and a tasting, sweet or savoury, along the way. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund, so it makes sense to lock in your place as soon as you know the date and cancel only if your plans change.

75185P1.intro: An hour beneath Chiaia, in the Bourbon tunnel. The standard route takes you through the cisterns of the old water system, the passages that served as air-raid shelters during the Second World War, and the storage areas where vintage cars and motorbikes have stood still for decades. On the walls and floors there are still objects left behind by the people who sheltered here from the bombs. The guide, in Italian or English, pieces together the stories of these spaces. With nearly three thousand reviews and a 4.9 rating, it’s one of the best-loved underground visits in the city.
cosaSiFa: You go down with the guide into the oldest part of the route, the great cisterns that were part of the area’s old water system. From there you move into the corridors that in the 20th century became an air-raid shelter: here the guide stops at the objects and marks left by those who spent bombing nights underground.

The last stretch is the most striking: passages full of vintage cars and motorbikes, left there and never moved again, with dust settling on them over the years. The tour lasts an hour and runs in a small group, up to 8 people, in Italian or English depending on the slot you booked.

The visit is told, not just shown: the guide reconstructs why the tunnel was dug, how its use changed over time and how the cars ended up there. That’s why it’s worth booking the slot in the language you understand best, Italian or English.
75185P1.perChi: Good for anyone short on time: in an hour you see one of the most unusual things in Naples without leaving the centre. Works with kids and teenagers, who are wowed by the abandoned cars, and with anyone who prefers 20th-century history to museums. The group is small, so you hear everything. If you don’t like enclosed spaces, think about it first: you’re underground for the whole visit.
75185P1.consiglio: The entrance is in Chiaia, a few minutes’ walk from Piazza del Plebiscito and the seafront: it pairs well with a morning between the Palazzo Reale and Castel dell’Ovo. Slots are small and sell out, so book a few days ahead and choose your language. It’s cooler underground than on the street: a light jumper in your bag won’t hurt.

faq.q: How long is the visit and how many people are there?
faq.a: The standard route lasts about an hour. Groups are small, up to 8 people, so the guide can answer questions and you can hear well even in the corridors. You book a specific slot with a start time.

faq.q: What language is the visit in?
